items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in North Dakota
items.meta: North Dakota Bakken and Three Forks mineral owners: if your royalty check has been sliding for a while, we'll price an offer against where the decline actually sits.

sections.html:
Bakken owners regularly ask the same question in different words: is the royalty check dropping because something's wrong, or is this just what a Bakken well does after year three.

North Dakota mineral owners are almost always Bakken and Three Forks owners, and if there's one thing to understand about this play it's that decline is the whole story. A Bakken well can produce more oil in its first eighteen months than most conventional wells produce in a decade, and then it settles into a much slower, longer tail. Your check today indicates roughly where the well sits on that curve, and that's the single biggest factor in what it's worth to sell.

The royalty desk reads royalty statements every day, and a North Dakota statement with a steep early decline followed by flattening is a completely different conversation than one still in year one of a sharp drop.

sections.title: Reading a Declining Bakken Check
sections.html:
A well in its first two years typically shows the steepest month-over-month drop, sometimes losing more than half its output within the first year alone. That's normal Bakken behavior, not a sign of a problem well. Once production flattens into its long tail, usually somewhere past year three or four, the remaining decline slows considerably and the well can keep paying at a modest, more predictable level for a long time.

When we quote an interest, we're trying to figure out where your well sits on that curve right now, because an offer priced off an early, still-declining check and one priced off a well that's already flattened out are two very different numbers.

sections.title: Core McKenzie and Mountrail County vs Outlying Counties
sections.html:
McKenzie, Mountrail, Williams, and Dunn counties sit in the thickest, most productive part of the Bakken and Three Forks, with the densest well spacing and the most multi-well pad development. Owners further out toward Divide, Burke, or McLean counties are often on somewhat thinner pay with less aggressive development, which shows up in both the size of the check and how much further drilling activity is likely.

Neither position is bad, but a core-county interest generally carries more near-term development upside, which is part of what we weigh alongside current production.

sections.title: Three Forks Behind Pipe
sections.html:
A number of North Dakota units have Bakken production actively flowing while a Three Forks well on the same spacing unit is permitted or drilled but not yet turned to sales, sometimes called behind pipe. If that's the case on your tract, it's worth knowing before you sell, since it represents real future production that isn't reflected in your current check at all.

We check state well records for exactly this kind of activity as part of any review, because it can materially change what a fair offer looks like.

sections.title: Force-Pooled Owners
sections.html:
North Dakota's forced pooling process brings unleased owners into a spacing unit under Industrial Comreview order rather than a negotiated lease, and the royalty terms that come with it can differ from what a neighbor negotiated privately. If you were force-pooled, we look at the order itself to understand exactly what royalty and cost terms apply to your interest before pricing an offer.

This comes up more often than people expect in North Dakota, particularly with older, smaller, or harder-to-locate mineral owners who never got leased the conventional way.

faqs.q: Your Bakken check has been shrinking every month. Should you sell now?
faqs.a: Depends where you are in the decline. If the well is still in its steep early years, waiting for it to flatten can sometimes mean a different value picture. If it's already leveled off at a lower, steady rate, that's often a more predictable time to price a sale. We'll tell you honestly which situation your statement shows.

faqs.q: What does behind pipe mean and does it affect your interest?
faqs.a: It means a well has been drilled and permitted on your spacing unit but hasn't started producing yet, usually because the operator is waiting to bring it online with other wells on the pad. It represents future production that isn't in your current check but should factor into value.

faqs.q: Is McKenzie County mineral rights worth more than Divide County?
faqs.a: Generally, core-county acreage in McKenzie, Mountrail, or Williams carries more near-term development potential and denser well spacing than more outlying counties, though every tract depends on its specific well history.

faqs.q: Do force-pooled owners still retain their minerals?
faqs.a: Yes, forced pooling brings you into the spacing unit's production and royalty terms under state order, it doesn't take away your ownership. We review the pooling order to confirm the exact terms before making an offer.

faqs.q: Does a Three Forks well behind pipe on your unit add value beyond your current check?
faqs.a: It can. A permitted or drilled but not yet producing Three Forks well represents real future volume that isn't reflected in your statement today, and we factor that potential into any offer once we've confirmed it through state well records.

faqs.q: How do you find out which county your North Dakota mineral rights are in?
faqs.a: Your division order or the legal description on an old deed will usually show it. If you only have a family name or a general area, we can often trace the tract through county and Industrial Comreview records from there.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Montana
items.meta: Montana mineral owners in Sheridan, Roosevelt, Richland, or the Powder River counties: get a cash offer read against your actual royalty statement, not a guess.

sections.html:
Years of reviewing Montana division orders show that two owners with the same acreage can have entirely different checks depending on which side of the state line they landed on.

Montana mineral owners fall into two camps and it matters which one you're in. Up in Sheridan, Roosevelt, and Richland counties you're on the flank of the Bakken, catching spillover from the North Dakota core but rarely the same intensity. Down in Powder River, Custer, and Rosebud counties you're more likely sitting on older coalbed methane gas or conventional oil that's been producing quietly for decades. Neither situation is bad. They're just different animals for pricing what a buyer will pay.

The review starts with the statement, not the map. A Montana check reveals more about spacing, operator behavior, and decline than any basin outline ever will.

sections.title: Bakken Flank vs. Core
sections.html:
If your acreage sits in eastern Sheridan or Roosevelt County, you're catching Bakken production but usually from wells drilled later in the play's development, often with wider spacing or thinner pay than what's common across the line in McKenzie County, North Dakota. That's not a knock on the interest, it just changes the math. Flank wells decline the same way core wells do, just from a lower starting point, so the value curve is compressed.

The royalty desk has evaluated flank interests where the owner assumed their check would behave like their cousin's in North Dakota and got frustrated when it didn't. Knowing which side of that line you're on before you talk numbers saves everybody time.

sections.title: Reading a Split Interest on a Small Montana Tract
sections.html:
A lot of Montana mineral ownership traces back to homestead-era severances, which means by the time it reaches you it's been divided among heirs multiple times over. Your decimal interest on the check might read something like 0.00312500, and that number alone tells an experienced buyer roughly what tract size and generation of split you're dealing with.

Before the royalty desk quotes anything, the file needs the actual decimal and the operator's name. Different operators in the same county can pay differently depending on their deduction practices, and that shows up in the net line before it shows up in anything the royalty desk could explain over the phone.

sections.title: Powder River County Coalbed and Conventional Gas
sections.html:
Powder River Basin coalbed methane in Montana never had the same volume of drilling as the Wyoming side, but there's a real base of older gas wells still on the books in Powder River, Custer, and Carter counties, plus scattered conventional oil going back to earlier development eras. Checks from this class of well tend to be small and steady rather than large and declining, which changes how the royalty desk evaluates a fair offer.

These are often the interests nobody in the family has looked at closely in years. A quick title and production pull usually tells us more than the owner expected, one way or the other.

sections.title: What We Look At Before We Quote a Montana Interest
sections.html:
We pull recent production history where it's public, cross-reference county assessor and clerk records for the legal description, and read your last several statements if you can send them. Montana counties vary in how digitized their records are, so older Sheridan and Roosevelt County filings sometimes take a courthouse call rather than an online pull.

Value on a Montana interest depends heavily on activity nearby, whether the well is still in its early decline or has flattened out, and whether there's any permitted offset activity that could change things. We'll walk you through what we found and how we got to a number before you decide anything.

faqs.q: Does your mineral rights value depend on which county you are in?
faqs.a: Yes, quite a bit. Sheridan and Roosevelt County flank-Bakken interests are typically priced against a different production curve than Powder River or Custer County coalbed and conventional interests. We look at your specific well history rather than a statewide average.

faqs.q: Your Montana check has been the same for years, is that normal?
faqs.a: For older coalbed and conventional wells, yes, flat checks over long stretches are common and usually mean the well has settled into a stable decline. For Bakken-adjacent wells, a flat check after early years can also mean production has leveled off rather than continuing to fall.

faqs.q: Can the royalty desk help with an inherited fractional interest when the legal description is unknown?
faqs.a: Usually. Send us whatever you have, a check stub, a division order, an old lease, and we can typically trace it through county records from there. A missing legal description slows things down, it doesn't stop them.

faqs.q: Is Powder River County coalbed gas worth less than Bakken minerals?
faqs.a: Not necessarily less, just different. Coalbed wells tend to have longer, flatter production tails at lower volumes, while Bakken wells start higher and decline faster. Depending on where each is in its life, either can come out ahead on a present-value basis.

faqs.q: Do you buy Montana minerals that aren't currently producing?
faqs.a: We evaluate those too, though the offer reflects that there's no current cash flow to base a decline projection on. Nearby permitting activity and historical production on the tract still matter.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Wyoming
items.meta: Wyoming mineral owners in the Powder River or Green River basins: checkerboard land patterns and federal units make these interests worth reading carefully.

sections.html:
Wyoming is the one state where the royalty desk asks about the section and township numbers before almost anything else, because the checkerboard pattern out here changes everything.

A lot of Wyoming's mineral ownership sits on what's called checkerboard land, alternating sections of federal, state, and private ownership that trace back to old railroad land grant patterns from the 1800s. Your neighbor's mineral rights a mile away might be federally administered while yours are private fee minerals, even though the surface looks continuous. That pattern shapes everything from leasing terms to who administers your unit.

Between that and Wyoming's split between Powder River Basin coalbed methane country and Green River Basin deep gas, the royalty desk never quotes a Wyoming interest without first understanding exactly where it sits and under what kind of unit.

sections.title: Wyoming's Checkerboard Land Pattern
sections.html:
The checkerboard traces back to 19th-century railroad grants, where alternating sections were given to the railroads and the sections between remained federal or later passed into state or private hands. That historical pattern still shapes mineral ownership today, meaning federal, state, and private minerals can sit adjacent to each other within the same township.

If your interest is private fee minerals surrounded by federal tracts, that's completely normal in Wyoming, but it's worth confirming exactly what you own before assuming your unit works the same way as a neighboring federal lease.

sections.title: Powder River Basin Coalbed Methane Owners
sections.html:
Wyoming's side of the Powder River Basin saw a major coalbed methane boom in the late 1990s and 2000s, with thousands of shallow wells drilled across Campbell, Johnson, and Sheridan counties. Many of those wells are now well into a long, low-volume production tail, and some have been shut in or plugged as the boom-era economics faded. If you're holding an older coalbed interest, the check today likely reflects that mature, declining stage.

We look at whether your specific well is still active, shut in, or plugged, since that status changes what's realistically being valued in a sale.

sections.title: Green River Basin Deep Gas
sections.html:
The Green River Basin in southwestern Wyoming carries some of the deepest, highest-pressure gas wells in our footprint, developed by operators willing to drill down through thick stacked pay in fields that have produced for decades. These wells behave differently than shallow coalbed gas, generally with steadier long-term output once past initial decline, and often tied to large, well-established units.

Owners here tend to have longer production histories to work from, which actually makes pricing more straightforward in some ways than a newer, less-established well.

sections.title: Federal Unit Owners
sections.html:
A significant share of Wyoming production happens on federal units administered under Bureau of Land Management lease terms, which can carry different royalty rates and administrative processes than a private Wyoming lease. If your interest sits within a federal unit, that affects both your statement's structure and what documentation is needed to complete a sale.

We identify this early since federal unit sales sometimes involve additional verification steps that a purely private Wyoming transaction doesn't.

faqs.q: What does checkerboard land mean for your Wyoming mineral rights?
faqs.a: It refers to Wyoming's historical pattern of alternating federal, state, and private land ownership tied to old railroad grants. It means your private mineral interest can sit right next to federally administered minerals, so it's worth confirming exactly what type of ownership yours is before assuming how your unit works.

faqs.q: Your Powder River Basin coalbed well seems to have stopped paying. What happened?
faqs.a: Many Powder River coalbed methane wells from the late 1990s and 2000s boom have reached the end of their economic life and been shut in or plugged. We check the specific well's current status before pricing, since that changes what's being valued.

faqs.q: Is Green River Basin gas worth more than Powder River coalbed gas?
faqs.a: Often the Green River's deep gas wells have steadier, longer production histories once past initial decline, while Powder River coalbed wells are frequently further along in decline or already shut in. We price against your specific well's actual production rather than a basin-wide assumption.

faqs.q: Does it matter if your interest is on a federal BLM unit?
faqs.a: Yes, federal units carry their own royalty structure and documentation requirements under Bureau of Land Management terms, which can add steps to a sale compared to a purely private Wyoming lease. We identify this early so it doesn't slow down closing.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your Wyoming minerals are private, state, or federal?
faqs.a: Your division order or lease usually identifies the lessor. If you're unsure, we can check the section, township, and range against county and BLM records to confirm exactly what type of ownership you hold.

faqs.q: Is a shut-in coalbed methane well still worth anything?
faqs.a: It can be, depending on whether the well could realistically be reactivated and what the historical production shows. We review the specific well's status and history rather than assuming a shut-in well has no remaining value.

faqs.q: Does the Green River Basin's remote location slow down a sale?
faqs.a: Not really on our end. We do the well and title research through Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Comreview and county records regardless of how remote the section is, so a sale can move at a normal pace even in less accessible parts of the basin.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Colorado
items.meta: Weld County DJ basin oil check or western slope Piceance gas royalty? Colorado plays behave differently. Get a fair offer built off your actual statements.

sections.html:
Where your Colorado check comes from matters more than almost anywhere else, an active Weld County oil well and a legacy Piceance gas well are two completely different situations.

Colorado splits pretty cleanly into two mineral-owning experiences. Around Greeley and across Weld County, the Denver-Julesburg basin is still an active horizontal drilling area, oil-heavy with associated gas, and operators there continue permitting new units, particularly on the fringes of existing development. If your check comes from that part of the state, you may still see real upside from infill drilling.

Out on the western slope, the Piceance basin around Garfield and Rio Blanco counties is a different story, a mature, mostly dry-gas field that was drilled hard in the 2000s and has seen very little new activity since gas prices pulled back. Owners there are almost always looking at a slow, steady decline with little chance of a new well changing that.

sections.title: DJ Basin Owners: Watch for New Unit Activity
sections.html:
Weld County is one of the few places in the country where operators are still actively permitting new horizontal wells, so a DJ basin interest carries a different kind of uncertainty than a legacy field. Your existing well may be declining normally while a new unit gets permitted next door that could bring your interest back up in a year or two.

That upside cuts both ways when you are deciding whether to sell. An offer on active DJ basin acreage typically accounts for both the current well's decline and any known permitted activity nearby, since that is real information available through the state's oil and gas comreview filings.

sections.title: Piceance Basin Checks Are a Different Read
sections.html:
If your statement shows a well operating in Garfield, Rio Blanco, or Mesa County with gas-only production, you are most likely in the Piceance, and the honest read is that new drilling there has been minimal for years. These are mature gas wells declining on a predictable curve with essentially no drilling program behind them right now.

Deductions on Piceance gas checks often run heavier than on an oil check because of the gathering and processing infrastructure required to move gas out of that part of the state, so a lower net number relative to gross volume is normal here, not a red flag.

sections.title: Colorado's Regulatory Environment Shapes Both Plays
sections.html:
Colorado has tightened setback and permitting rules over the past several years, particularly around populated areas of Weld County. That has slowed, but not stopped, new DJ basin permitting, and it is worth knowing that regulatory friction is part of why some units take longer to get drilled than they used to.

For Piceance owners, regulation is less of a factor than simple economics, dry gas in a remote part of the state competing against cheaper gas basins elsewhere. Either way, it is useful context when you are trying to understand why your check moves the way it does.

sections.title: Getting an Offer on Either Type of Interest
sections.html:
Send your most recent statements and we will identify which basin and county your interest sits in from the operator name and well information. DJ basin offers factor in nearby permitted activity where it exists; Piceance offers are built almost entirely off documented decline, since new drilling is not a realistic near-term factor there.

From there, closing runs through a standard mineral deed and a title check at the county clerk's office where the interest is recorded, usually Weld County for DJ basin interests or Garfield, Rio Blanco, or Mesa County for Piceance interests. Most closings wrap up within a few weeks once ownership and any co-owner details are confirmed.

faqs.q: Is there still active drilling in the DJ basin?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly in Weld County, where operators continue permitting new horizontal wells, though setback rules and local approvals have slowed the pace compared to the 2010s peak.

faqs.q: Why is your Piceance basin gas check smaller than you expected?
faqs.a: Gathering and processing costs for gas moving out of the Piceance tend to run higher than for oil production elsewhere, which shows up as larger deductions between the gross production volume and your net royalty.

faqs.q: Should you wait to sell if your well is in an active drilling area?
faqs.a: That depends on your own timeline and risk tolerance. Active areas carry real upside potential from new units, but also carry the uncertainty of permitting delays, so we walk through what is currently filed near your interest before you decide.

faqs.q: How do you know which basin your Colorado interest is in?
faqs.a: The operator name and well or unit information on your statement will tell us. Weld County interests are almost always DJ basin; Garfield, Rio Blanco, or Mesa County interests are almost always Piceance.

faqs.q: Do Colorado's setback rules affect the value of your interest?
faqs.a: They can, mainly by slowing how quickly nearby permits move from filing to drilling. It is a factor we consider for DJ basin acreage specifically, since it affects how much weight nearby permitted activity should carry in an offer.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Texas
items.meta: Texas mineral owners in the Permian, Eagle Ford, Haynesville, Barnett, or Anadarko: we start by figuring out which play is actually paying your check.

sections.html:
Ask the royalty desk about Texas mineral rights and the first question is always which Texas, because West Texas, South Texas, and East Texas don't have much in common besides the state line.

Texas is the biggest mineral rights state the royalty desk reviews, and it's really five or six different plays wearing one name. A Permian Basin owner in Midland or Reeves County is looking at a completely different well profile than an Eagle Ford owner in Karnes County or a Haynesville owner up near Harrison County. Before the royalty desk can support a number, the file needs to identify which play, which county, and ideally which operator you're dealing with.

That's not a stall tactic, it's just how Texas actually works. The state's size means a statewide answer is almost always the wrong answer for your specific tract.

sections.title: Which Play Is Paying Your Check
sections.html:
Your division order or lease should name the well, and from there county records tell us the play. If you're not sure, the mix of products on your statement is a decent clue, heavy oil with some gas points toward Permian or Eagle Ford, while a stream that's almost entirely gas with little liquid content often points toward Haynesville or Barnett.

Once we know the play, we pull well-level production rather than relying on general assumptions about how that basin performs, since individual wells vary widely even within the same formation.

sections.title: Permian Basin Owners (West Texas)
sections.html:
Midland, Reeves, Loving, Ward, and the surrounding counties sit in the most actively developed oil play in the country, with multi-bench horizontal drilling and, in many spots, ongoing permitting for additional wells on existing units. Permian interests generally carry the strongest near-term development potential of any Texas play we see, which is a real factor in pricing beyond just current production.

We check Railroad Comreview permits for your specific unit as part of any Permian offer, since undrilled locations already permitted can matter as much as what's currently producing.

sections.title: Eagle Ford Owners (South Texas)
sections.html:
Karnes, DeWitt, La Salle, and neighboring counties made up one of the earliest major horizontal shale plays, and a lot of Eagle Ford wells are now well into their production life with established, if declining, output. Owners here are often deciding between holding a mature, steady-if-shrinking check or selling into an offer priced against that known decline trajectory.

We look closely at how far along the curve your specific well sits, since Eagle Ford wells span a wide range of ages and remaining life at this point in the play's history.

sections.title: East Texas Haynesville and Legacy Barnett
sections.html:
Harrison, Panola, and Shelby counties sit in the Texas side of the Haynesville, a dry gas play that's highly sensitive to natural gas pricing cycles, with activity ramping up and down depending on where gas prices sit. Further north, the Barnett Shale around Fort Worth was one of the original shale gas plays and is now almost entirely legacy production, older wells on long, flat declines with limited new drilling.

Anadarko Basin acreage in the Texas Panhandle carries its own mix of older conventional production and some newer horizontal activity, and we price it the same way, against the specific well rather than the play's reputation.

sections.title: Texas Railroad Comreview Records
sections.html:
Texas keeps unusually thorough public well and production records through the Railroad Comreview, which actually works in your favor when selling, since we can verify a well's history without relying entirely on your statements. That said, county-level title work still matters for confirming the actual chain of ownership on your tract.

We handle both pieces so you're not stuck gathering documents you may not have on hand.

faqs.q: How do you know which play your Texas mineral rights are in?
faqs.a: Your division order or lease will typically name the well and county, which we can cross-reference against Railroad Comreview records. If you're unsure, send us what you have and we'll identify the play before quoting.

faqs.q: Is Permian Basin acreage worth more than Eagle Ford or Haynesville?
faqs.a: Generally the Permian carries more near-term development potential given current drilling activity, but a mature, well-performing Eagle Ford or Haynesville interest can still be a strong asset. We price against your specific well's history and remaining potential rather than a blanket ranking of plays.

faqs.q: Your Barnett Shale check has been flat and small for years. Is it still worth selling?
faqs.a: Often yes, legacy Barnett wells that have settled into a long, flat decline can still have real value, priced against that steady, lower-volume tail rather than early-life production assumptions.

faqs.q: Do you check Railroad Comreview records before making an offer?
faqs.a: Yes, Texas's public well and production data through the Railroad Comreview is a standard part of how we verify a well's history and current status before pricing any Texas interest.

faqs.q: Can minerals in more than one Texas play be evaluated as one package?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. We evaluate each tract on its own production and location, then can put together a single offer covering multiple counties or plays if that's simpler for you.

faqs.q: What if you only have partial paperwork on your Texas mineral rights?
faqs.a: That's common, especially with older or inherited interests. Between Railroad Comreview well records and county deed records, we can usually piece together enough to move forward even with incomplete files on your end.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Oklahoma
items.meta: Oklahoma pooled-unit mineral owners in the SCOOP, STACK, Anadarko, Arkoma, or Osage: we start with your decimal interest and build the offer from there.

sections.html:
The first thing the royalty desk requests from an Oklahoma owner isn't the county, it's the decimal on the check, because that number is where the real conversation starts.

Oklahoma runs mostly on pooled spacing units, which means your royalty check almost never reflects a single well sitting on your own tract. Instead you're getting a decimal share, your net revenue interest, of everything produced from a larger unit that may cover 640 or 1,280 acres and include several wells. Understanding that decimal, and how it was calculated, is the starting point for any real conversation about what your interest is worth.

Owners sometimes assume their check was small because their well wasn't producing much, when the real answer was just a small decimal on a very productive unit. Getting that distinction right changes the entire offer.

sections.title: Your Decimal Interest on an Oklahoma Pooled Unit
sections.html:
Oklahoma spacing units are typically set by Corporation Comreview order, and your net revenue interest is your mineral acreage divided by the total unit acreage, multiplied by your royalty rate. A tiny-looking decimal like 0.00195 isn't unusual on a 1,280-acre unit if your family holds a modest tract, and it doesn't mean the unit itself is underperforming.

We ask for a division order or recent check stub early specifically to see that decimal, since it tells us your share size independent of how the unit as a whole is producing.

sections.title: SCOOP and STACK Owners
sections.html:
The SCOOP and STACK plays across central Oklahoma have seen dense, multi-bench horizontal development for years now, often with several wells targeting different formations under the same surface acreage. If you're in one of these plays, it's worth checking whether there's permitted but undrilled activity on your unit, since additional wells can be added to an existing unit well after your first check arrives.

We look at Corporation Comreview filings for exactly this before pricing, because a unit with active permitting behaves differently going forward than one that's fully developed and declining.

sections.title: Osage County's Different Rules
sections.html:
Osage County operates under a different regulatory structure than the rest of Oklahoma, with mineral rights held in trust for the Osage Nation and administered through federal processes rather than the state Corporation Comreview. If your interest is in Osage County, the paperwork and approval process for a sale is genuinely different, and we handle it accordingly rather than treating it like a standard Oklahoma transaction.

This is one of the few places in our footprint where the process itself, beyond the geology, changes materially.

sections.title: Arkoma Basin Coalbed Gas and Legacy Anadarko Wells
sections.html:
Southeastern Oklahoma's Arkoma Basin has a long history of coalbed methane and conventional gas production, generally older and more slowly declining than the horizontal plays further west. The western Anadarko Basin similarly carries decades of legacy conventional production alongside newer horizontal activity in spots. Both tend to produce steadier, more predictable checks than a newly drilled SCOOP or STACK well still working through its early decline.

We price these the same careful way, against actual production history rather than assuming everything in the state behaves like the newer plays.

faqs.q: Why is your decimal interest so small if you own a decent amount of land?
faqs.a: Oklahoma spacing units can cover 640 to 1,280 acres or more, and your decimal reflects your mineral acreage as a fraction of the whole unit. A small decimal on a large, productive unit can still add up to a solid check.

faqs.q: Can more wells be added to your Oklahoma unit after you start getting checks?
faqs.a: Yes, especially in the SCOOP and STACK where operators often develop multiple benches over time. We check Corporation Comreview permitting activity to see if that's likely before pricing an offer.

faqs.q: Is selling mineral rights in Osage County different from the rest of Oklahoma?
faqs.a: Yes. Osage County minerals are held in trust for the Osage Nation and involve a different approval process than standard state transactions. We handle Osage County sales with the appropriate additional steps built in.

faqs.q: Your Arkoma Basin check is small and hasn't changed in years. Is that a bad sign?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Arkoma coalbed and conventional wells often settle into a long, flat, low-volume production tail, which shows up as a steady rather than declining check for extended periods.

faqs.q: How do you confirm your exact decimal interest before talking to a buyer?
faqs.a: Your division order will show it directly. If you don't have one on hand, a recent check stub usually lists it too, and if neither is available we can typically pull it from Corporation Comreview and county records once we know the well or unit name.

faqs.q: Do you buy legacy Anadarko Basin conventional interests, or only newer SCOOP and STACK wells?
faqs.a: We buy both. Legacy Anadarko interests are priced against their own steady, mature production history rather than compared to newer horizontal wells, which behave very differently.

faqs.q: How quickly can an Oklahoma mineral sale close?
faqs.a: Once we have your division order and can confirm the decimal and title, most Oklahoma closings move fairly quickly, typically a matter of weeks rather than months, though older or more fractured title chains can take longer.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in New Mexico
items.meta: New Mexico mineral owners in Lea, Eddy, or the San Juan Basin: get an offer priced against your actual well activity, whether you're in the Delaware or legacy San Juan gas.

sections.html:
The royalty desk has priced New Mexico interests on both ends of the state and they might as well be different states entirely once you get past the map.

New Mexico mineral owners are usually in one of two very different situations depending on which part of the state they're in. Lea and Eddy counties sit in the Delaware Basin, the hottest corner of the Permian, with dense modern drilling and deep multi-bench development. The San Juan Basin in the northwest corner is a different story: an older, mostly gas-producing basin that's been declining for years off a much slower, more conventional development pattern.

The royalty desk does not quote a New Mexico interest until the file identifies which basin, and honestly which part of which basin, it sits in. The gap in value between the two can be enormous even though both are technically in-state.

sections.title: Two Basins, Two Very Different Checks
sections.html:
A Delaware Basin owner in Lea or Eddy County is typically looking at active multi-well pad development, sometimes stacked across several benches on the same section, which means new wells can come online on your tract years after the first one. That ongoing development potential is a real part of what a buyer factors into an offer.

A San Juan Basin owner in Rio Arriba or San Juan County is more likely holding an interest in older gas wells that have been on a long, gentle decline for a decade or more, with limited chance of new drilling changing that trajectory. Both are legitimate, valuable interests. They just get priced against different assumptions.

sections.title: Lea and Eddy County Delaware Basin Owners
sections.html:
If your check comes from Lea or Eddy County, the review questions cover about spacing unit size, how many wells are currently producing on your tract versus permitted but not yet drilled, and which operator holds the lease. Operators in this corner of the Permian have been aggressive about downspacing and multi-bench development, which is generally good news for future value but also means your current check may not reflect what's still coming.

We look at permits filed with the Oil Conservation Division alongside your production history to get a fuller picture before quoting.

sections.title: San Juan Basin Legacy Gas Owners
sections.html:
San Juan Basin wells are largely mature, and a lot of the acreage was developed decades ago under different spacing and unitization rules than you'd see in a newer play. Checks here tend to be smaller and steadier, reflecting wells well past their peak. That's not a reason to assume the interest has no value, it just changes what a fair offer looks like.

We also see a fair number of San Juan interests tied up in old coalbed methane units from the basin's development boom in the 1990s and 2000s, which have their own pooling quirks worth understanding before you sell.

sections.title: State Trust Land and Nonparticipating Royalty Interests
sections.html:
New Mexico has a large amount of state trust land, and mineral interests near or adjoining those tracts sometimes carry unusual provisions tied to how the state manages its own royalty. If your interest is a nonparticipating royalty rather than a full mineral fee, that also changes what rights transfer in a sale, since you don't hold the leasing or bonus rights the underlying mineral owner does.

We sort out which kind of interest you actually hold as part of the review, since the deed language often doesn't make it obvious at a glance.

faqs.q: Is Delaware Basin acreage in Lea and Eddy County worth more than San Juan Basin gas?
faqs.a: Generally yes on a per-acre basis, given the pace and density of Permian development, but the honest answer depends on your specific well's production, remaining development potential, and how far along the decline curve it already is.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a mineral interest and a nonparticipating royalty interest in New Mexico?
faqs.a: A mineral fee owner controls leasing decisions and receives bonus and rental payments along with royalty. A nonparticipating royalty interest only receives a royalty share and has no say in leasing. We identify which one your deed actually grants before quoting.

faqs.q: Your San Juan Basin check has dropped a lot over the past few years. Is that normal?
faqs.a: Yes, most San Juan gas wells are decades into production and have been on a long decline. That doesn't mean the interest is worthless, it means the remaining value reflects a lower, steadier tail rather than early-life volumes.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests near New Mexico state trust land?
faqs.a: We do, though we review the specific lease and unit terms closely since state trust land arrangements can carry different provisions than private mineral leases nearby.

faqs.q: How fast is Delaware Basin activity moving in Lea and Eddy counties?
faqs.a: It varies with commodity prices and individual operator programs, but the Delaware has consistently drawn dense multi-well pad development for years. We check current permits rather than relying on last year's activity level when pricing your specific unit.

faqs.q: What documents do you need to make a New Mexico offer?
faqs.a: A recent check stub or division order, any lease or deed you have, and the legal description if you know it. We can fill in most gaps through Lea, Eddy, or San Juan county records if paperwork is missing.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Pennsylvania
items.meta: Pennsylvania Marcellus mineral owners: if post-production deductions have been eating your gas check, we'll price an offer against your net line, not the headline price.

sections.html:
Nearly every Pennsylvania owner who contacts the royalty desk has the same complaint before they even say hello: the price of gas went up and their check didn't.

Pennsylvania Marcellus checks carry more deduction line items than almost any other state the royalty desk reviews, and that's not an accident. A lot of Pennsylvania leases, especially older ones signed during the play's early boom years, gave operators broad room to deduct gathering, compression, processing, and transportation costs before calculating your royalty. That means the wellhead price you read about in the news and the net price on your statement can be two very different numbers.

Before the royalty desk quotes a Pennsylvania interest, the file needs the deduction detail on your statement, beyond the bottom-line total. That's where the real story is.

sections.title: Why Your Check Looks Smaller Than the Price You Read About
sections.html:
Post-production costs in Pennsylvania are typically netted out before your royalty is calculated, covering the gas's trip from the wellhead through gathering lines, compression, processing, and pipeline transportation to market. Depending on your lease language, some or all of these costs land on your side of the ledger rather than the operator's, and they can take a real bite out of an otherwise strong gas price.

We read the deduction breakdown on your statement as part of any offer, since a lease that shifts heavy post-production costs onto the royalty owner changes the effective net price meaningfully, and that matters for what the interest is worth going forward.

sections.title: Marcellus vs Utica Depth Rights
sections.html:
In parts of northeastern and southwestern Pennsylvania, the Marcellus isn't the only formation with development potential, the deeper Utica shale sits below it and in some cases has separate leasing and drilling activity. Whether your original lease or deed covers just the Marcellus or all formations down to a stated depth matters if there's ever additional development below your current producing zone.

We check depth language on older leases specifically because Pennsylvania has more of this layered-formation activity than most states we cover.

sections.title: Northeast vs Southwest Pennsylvania
sections.html:
The northeast counties, Susquehanna, Bradford, Wyoming, tend to produce dry gas with strong volumes but no liquids premium. The southwest, around Washington and Greene counties, sits closer to a wetter window with some natural gas liquids content, which can add value to the stream. Knowing which region your acreage sits in shapes what a realistic offer looks like from the start.

Well density and operator activity also differ meaningfully between the two regions, which factors into how we think about remaining development potential.

sections.title: Leases Signed But Never Developed
sections.html:
A fair number of Pennsylvania owners signed leases during the boom years of the late 2000s and early 2010s that were never actually drilled, and those leases have since expired, renewed, or in some cases sit in a murky status the owner isn't sure about. If that's your situation, your minerals may be unleased right now even though you remember signing something years ago.

We check current lease status through county records before assuming anything about what rights you're actually selling.

faqs.q: Why did the price of gas go up but your Pennsylvania royalty check didn't?
faqs.a: Most likely post-production cost deductions. Many Pennsylvania leases allow operators to deduct gathering, compression, processing, and transportation costs before calculating your royalty, which can offset a rising wellhead price. We review your deduction detail as part of any offer.

faqs.q: Does your lease cover the Utica shale below the Marcellus?
faqs.a: It depends on the depth language in your specific lease or deed. Some Pennsylvania leases are limited to the Marcellus formation while others extend to all formations to a stated depth. We check this since it affects future development potential.

faqs.q: Is your Pennsylvania interest still under lease if it was never drilled?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Leases signed but never developed during the early Marcellus boom have in many cases expired or moved to a different status. We verify current lease standing through county records before pricing a sale.

faqs.q: Are northeast Pennsylvania and southwest Pennsylvania Marcellus wells valued differently?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Northeast counties tend toward higher-volume dry gas while southwest counties see some natural gas liquids content, and well density differs by region. We price against your specific well's production and location rather than a statewide figure.

faqs.q: Can you still sell if your lease has a long list of post-production deductions?
faqs.a: Yes. Heavy deductions lower your net price but don't stop a sale, they just factor into what a fair offer looks like. We build the deduction structure into the pricing rather than treating your net check as the whole story.

faqs.q: What paperwork do you need for a Pennsylvania mineral rights sale?
faqs.a: A recent statement, your lease if you have it, and any deed showing how you acquired the interest. If pieces are missing, county recorder records in your township usually fill the gaps.

faqs.q: Is a Marcellus well still worth selling once it's several years past peak?
faqs.a: Often yes, a mature well that's settled into a longer, flatter decline can still carry real value, priced against that steadier remaining production rather than early-life volumes. We look at your specific well's history before deciding what a fair number looks like.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in West Virginia
items.meta: West Virginia mineral owners holding an old severed estate in Marcellus or Utica country: we do the deed research a century-old severance usually needs.

sections.html:
West Virginia has more hundred-year-old severed mineral deeds than any state the royalty desk reviews, and tracing one of those back to a living owner is half the job.

West Virginia's coal, oil, and gas history goes back well over a century, and a lot of mineral ownership in the state was severed from the surface during that early era, sometimes for a few dollars an acre, long before anyone imagined Marcellus and Utica development. Those old severances got divided among heirs generation after generation, which means the person holding a fractional interest today is often several generations removed from whoever originally sold the minerals off.

That history is exactly why West Virginia title work looks different from a newer state. It's slower, it's more document-heavy, and it's something we've done often enough to move through efficiently.

sections.title: West Virginia's Old Severed Estates
sections.html:
A severed mineral estate means the mineral rights were split off from surface ownership at some point, sometimes decades before oil and gas development made those minerals valuable. In West Virginia, this frequently happened in the late 1800s or early 1900s tied to coal, timber, or early oil interests, with the mineral portion then passing through generations of heirs, sometimes without anyone updating the county record along the way.

If you've inherited a fractional interest and don't have a clean modern deed, that's completely normal here. We're set up to trace it.

sections.title: Marcellus Depth vs Utica Depth Rights
sections.html:
Because West Virginia's mineral history predates modern shale development by so long, older deeds sometimes used depth language that wasn't written with the Marcellus or the deeper Utica in mind, or in some cases only conveyed rights to specific formations known at the time. Whether your interest covers both formations, just one, or something more ambiguous depends entirely on the specific deed language.

We read that language carefully, since it determines what you actually have the right to sell and what an operator can develop under an existing lease.

sections.title: Northern Panhandle vs Southern West Virginia
sections.html:
The Northern Panhandle counties, Marshall, Wetzel, Ohio, sit in some of the most active Marcellus and Utica development in the state, with dense modern horizontal drilling. Southern West Virginia's production leans more toward older, shallower conventional gas wells alongside the region's long coal history. Both regions have real value, but the development pace and well profile differ enough that we price them on separate assumptions.

We ask which part of the state you're in early, since it changes what questions we ask next.

sections.title: Tracking Down a Century-Old Deed
sections.html:
West Virginia county clerk offices hold deed books going back well over a hundred years, and finding the original severance instrument, then following every subsequent transfer or probate down to you, can take real research time. We handle this as a standard part of our process rather than asking you to produce documents you likely don't have.

If you have even fragments, an old letter, a partial deed, a family name, that's often enough for us to pick up the trail at the courthouse.

faqs.q: Can the royalty desk help when an owner has family knowledge but no West Virginia deed?
faqs.a: Yes, this is common in West Virginia given how old many severances are. We can typically trace ownership through county clerk records starting from whatever fragments of information you have, a family name, an approximate location, an old document.

faqs.q: Does your old deed cover the Marcellus and the Utica, or just one?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific depth and formation language in your deed, which can vary widely on older West Virginia instruments. We review this carefully since it determines what rights you actually hold.

faqs.q: Is Northern Panhandle acreage worth more than southern West Virginia?
faqs.a: Generally the Northern Panhandle has seen denser modern Marcellus and Utica development, which can support stronger near-term value, but southern West Virginia interests with steady conventional production still have real worth. We price against your specific well and history.

faqs.q: How long does title research take on an old West Virginia severed estate?
faqs.a: It varies with how many generations and transfers are involved, but it's routine work for us. We start it right after an initial conversation so it doesn't hold up your offer any longer than necessary.

faqs.q: Your family owns a small fractional share split among several cousins. Can you buy just your piece?
faqs.a: Yes, we can typically buy an individual owner's fractional share without requiring every co-owner to sell. We confirm your exact percentage through the deed and probate chain before making an offer.

faqs.q: Does West Virginia coal severance affect your oil and gas mineral rights?
faqs.a: It can, since some older deeds bundled coal, oil, and gas together while others split them out separately. We read the specific severance language on your deed to confirm what you actually hold before pricing anything.

faqs.q: Can you buy a West Virginia interest that's currently in a dispute among heirs?
faqs.a: Sometimes, depending on the nature of the dispute. We'll be honest early if a title issue needs to be resolved through probate or court before a clean sale can close, rather than taking your file and letting it stall out later.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Ohio
items.meta: Ohio Utica mineral owners in Belmont, Monroe, or Carroll County: get an offer priced to your check's actual liquids content and pooling order, not a flat rate.

sections.html:
Two Ohio owners can hold the same acreage size in adjoining counties and get paid completely differently depending on which window their rock sits in.

Ohio's Utica play runs through a fairly narrow band of eastern counties, and where you sit within that band matters more than almost anything else about your interest. Belmont and Monroe counties tend to sit in the wet gas and condensate window, which usually means a richer, more valuable stream than pure dry gas. Carroll and parts of Harrison County were early development hotspots and carry some of the longest production histories in the play.

The royalty desk asks about the county and production window first, because the answer changes the entire pricing conversation.

sections.title: Ohio's Utica Windows
sections.html:
The Utica shale isn't uniform across eastern Ohio. Moving from west to east and north to south, the rock shifts from dry gas to a wet gas and condensate window to, in a few spots, an oil-richer window. Wet gas and condensate production typically brings a higher-value stream than dry gas alone, since natural gas liquids get priced and sold separately and usually command more.

If you're not sure which window your acreage sits in, your statement usually gives it away, a mix of gas, NGL, and condensate line items points to wet gas, while a check that's essentially all gas volume points to a dry gas well.

sections.title: Belmont and Monroe County Owners
sections.html:
These two counties have seen some of the most productive Utica wells in the state, often with strong initial production and a meaningful liquids component. Owners here tend to have more leverage in an offer conversation simply because the underlying production supports it, but the specific well's age and current rate still drive the number more than the county name does.

We pull well-level production data where available rather than pricing off a county average, since two wells a few miles apart in the same county can perform very differently.

sections.title: Ohio's Mandatory Pooling Process
sections.html:
Ohio allows operators to bring unleased or non-consenting mineral owners into a drilling unit through the state's mandatory pooling process, administered through the Chief of the Division of Oil and Gas Resources Management. If your interest was pooled this way rather than under a privately negotiated lease, the royalty terms come from that order rather than a lease you signed, and they're worth reviewing closely.

We check for this as part of any title review since it changes what documents govern your interest and what royalty rate actually applies.

sections.title: What Slows an Ohio Closing
sections.html:
Eastern Ohio mineral ownership frequently traces back through multiple generations of family farmland, and severed mineral interests here sometimes go back far enough that tracking the chain of title takes real courthouse work in the county recorder's office. That's routine for us, but it's worth knowing upfront that an Ohio closing can take a bit longer than a state with more recently established ownership records.

We start the title work immediately after you accept an offer so it doesn't sit as a bottleneck later.

faqs.q: Does it matter if your Ohio well produces wet gas or dry gas?
faqs.a: Yes, meaningfully. Wet gas and condensate wells generally produce a higher-value combined stream than dry gas alone because natural gas liquids are sold separately and typically bring more per unit than gas.

faqs.q: What is Ohio mandatory pooling and does it affect what you own?
faqs.a: It's a state process that can bring unleased mineral owners into a drilling unit under an order rather than a private lease. It doesn't take away ownership, but it does set the royalty terms that apply, which we review as part of any offer.

faqs.q: Why does your Belmont County check look different from your cousin's in Carroll County?
faqs.a: Different wells, different vintages, and possibly different windows of the Utica formation. Even within the same play, well-level production and liquids content vary enough that county alone doesn't predict your check.

faqs.q: How long does an Ohio mineral rights closing typically take?
faqs.a: It depends on how clean the title chain is. Ohio interests with older, multi-generation severances can take longer to research than more recently established ownership, though we begin title work right away to keep things moving.

faqs.q: Are Carroll County wells still worth buying given how long they've produced?
faqs.a: Often yes. Carroll County was an early Utica hotspot, and many of those wells have settled into a steady, well-understood production tail. A long, documented history can actually make pricing more straightforward than a newer, still-declining well elsewhere in the play.

faqs.q: What if your Ohio mineral rights were leased decades ago under a coal-era deed?
faqs.a: That's common in eastern Ohio, where oil and gas rights were sometimes bundled with older coal severances. We read the specific deed language to confirm what was actually conveyed before pricing a sale.

faqs.q: Do you buy Ohio interests that are still leased but not yet drilled?
faqs.a: Yes, we evaluate those, though the offer reflects that there's no current production yet. Nearby permitting activity, the operator's development pace in your county, and how much time is left on the lease term all factor into the number.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Louisiana
items.meta: Active Haynesville gas well, quiet Tuscaloosa Marine Shale acreage, or legacy Gulf Coast oil interest? Three different Louisiana plays, three different offers.

sections.html:
Where your Louisiana acreage sits inside the play matters as much as which play it's in, core Haynesville acreage behaves nothing like its flank, and neither behaves like Gulf Coast legacy production.

Louisiana carries three distinct royalty stories depending on where your interest sits. The Haynesville shale, running through Caddo, Bossier, and DeSoto parishes, is genuinely active today, driven largely by LNG export demand for natural gas, and operators are still permitting and drilling new wells in the core of the play. If your check is Haynesville, you may be looking at one of the few gas plays in the country with real near-term drilling activity behind it.

South of there, the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale, spanning parishes near the Louisiana-Mississippi line, told a different story. Early operators drilled a wave of wells starting around 2013, ran into difficult geology and high costs, and mostly pulled back within a few years. Most TMS acreage today sits quiet, with owners holding leases or small legacy production rather than active drilling. And along the coast, Gulf Coast parishes like Cameron and Vermilion carry a much older history of conventional oil and gas, much of it declining steadily for decades.

sections.title: Core Haynesville vs. the Flank
sections.html:
Not all Haynesville acreage is equal. Core counties, Caddo, Bossier, DeSoto, sit over the thickest, most productive part of the shale and continue to see active drilling. Flank acreage on the edges of the play has historically drawn less operator interest and thinner results, even within the same general region.

That distinction matters directly for an offer. Core Haynesville production with recent drilling nearby is priced very differently than flank acreage with an older, quieter well and no permits filed nearby, and we tell owners plainly which situation they are in before any number comes up.

sections.title: Tuscaloosa Marine Shale: A Boom That Mostly Didn't Happen
sections.html:
If you hold TMS acreage, the honest history is that the play underperformed the early hype. High well costs and inconsistent results led most operators to scale back drilling within a few years of the initial rush, and large-scale development that was once expected simply has not materialized since.

That does not make a TMS interest worthless, but it does mean valuing it requires an honest look at whatever production history actually exists rather than pricing off the optimism that surrounded the play a decade ago.

sections.title: Gulf Coast Legacy Production Reads Like an Old Field
sections.html:
Cameron, Vermilion, and other Gulf Coast parishes carry decades of conventional oil and gas history, much of it mature fields in steady, well-understood decline. These checks tend to be smaller and more predictable than a shale check, closer in character to legacy production you would find in Texas's older fields.

Owners here are often multiple generations removed from whoever signed the original lease, and interests can be fractional across several heirs, which is worth accounting for before assuming your offer will reflect a full undivided interest.

sections.title: Getting an Offer Built for Your Specific Play
sections.html:
Send us your most recent statement and, if you have it, the well or unit name. That tells us immediately whether you are in core or flank Haynesville, TMS, or a Gulf Coast legacy field, and each of those gets evaluated on its own recent production history and, where relevant, nearby permitted activity.

Closing runs through a mineral deed and a title check at the parish clerk of court where the interest is recorded, and timelines are typically a few weeks once ownership and any heirship questions are sorted out.

faqs.q: Is the Haynesville shale still being actively drilled?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly in the core counties of Caddo, Bossier, and DeSoto parish, where LNG export demand has kept drilling activity going in recent years, more than in most other gas plays nationally.

faqs.q: What happened to the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale?
faqs.a: Early operators drilled aggressively starting around 2013 but ran into difficult geology and high costs, and most scaled back development within a few years. Large-scale drilling in the play has not resumed since.

faqs.q: Why is your Gulf Coast Louisiana check so much smaller than a Haynesville check?
faqs.a: Gulf Coast parishes carry much older, more mature conventional production that has been declining for decades, so checks there tend to be smaller and steadier than newer shale gas production further north.

faqs.q: How do you know if your acreage is core or flank Haynesville?
faqs.a: The parish and section-township-range on your statement or lease, along with nearby permitted well activity, tell us where your acreage sits within the play. We check this before discussing any offer.

faqs.q: Does LNG export demand actually affect what your Haynesville royalty is worth?
faqs.a: It has been a real driver of continued drilling interest in the play, since export terminals along the Gulf Coast create demand for the gas Haynesville wells produce. That said, offers are still built from your specific well's documented production, not broader market narratives.

faqs.q: Your Louisiana interest is held through a succession that was never completed. Can you still sell?
faqs.a: It is workable, but a Louisiana succession, the state's version of probate, needs to be resolved or at least underway before a clean transfer can close. We can walk you through what that typically involves for a mineral interest specifically.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Arkansas
items.meta: Fayetteville shale gas check declining? Legacy Smackover oil interest? We buy Arkansas mineral and royalty interests and explain the offer in plain terms.

sections.html:
Arkansas owners tend to fall into one of two very different check profiles, a declining Fayetteville shale gas well or a legacy Smackover stripper oil interest, and a third one is starting to show up on statements now.

The Fayetteville shale, concentrated across Van Buren, Conway, Cleburne, and White counties, was one of the earlier dry-gas shale plays, drilled hard from roughly 2005 through 2012 and largely left alone since. If your check comes from that field, you are almost certainly years into a decline curve with essentially no new drilling behind it.

Further south, the Smackover trend around El Dorado and Union County is a different animal entirely, legacy oil and gas production going back generations, much of it on stripper wells producing small, steady volumes. And in the last few years, brine operations tied to that same Smackover formation have started producing lithium as a byproduct, which is showing up as an entirely new line on some owners' statements.

sections.title: The Fayetteville Shale Is Past Its Peak
sections.html:
Almost nobody is drilling new Fayetteville wells today. Operators shifted capital to other basins years ago, and what remains is mature production sliding down a well-documented decline curve. That is not a knock on the field, it simply means the upside case, new pad drilling reviving your unit, is not realistic for most owners here.

If your statement shows gas volumes that have fallen steadily for several years running, that pattern is normal for this play and it is exactly the kind of production history we use to build an offer, rather than trying to price against hope for a rebound.

sections.title: Smackover Checks Read Differently Than Shale Checks
sections.html:
South Arkansas Smackover production tends to be older wells with smaller gross volumes but often longer histories of stable, low-decline output. Deductions on these older leases can vary quite a bit depending on when the lease was originally signed, since older Arkansas leases sometimes carry different cost-bearing language than anything drilled in the last twenty years.

If you inherited a Smackover interest and are not sure whether your lease requires you to bear post-production costs, that is worth pulling the original document for. It changes how your net royalty is calculated and, in turn, how an offer on that interest should be built.

sections.title: The New Lithium Brine Line Item
sections.html:
A handful of operators in the Smackover trend, especially around the Arkansas-Louisiana border, are now producing lithium from the same brine that has historically just been a byproduct of oil and gas operations. If a lithium royalty term has started appearing on your statement, that is genuinely new activity, not an accounting change, and it can meaningfully affect what your interest is worth.

Lithium brine royalty terms are new enough in Arkansas that lease and royalty language is still standardizing across operators, so we look at the specific royalty clause covering that production before including it in any offer discussion.

sections.title: Selling a Fayetteville or Smackover Interest
sections.html:
For a declining Fayetteville gas interest, the case for selling usually comes down to trading a shrinking monthly check for a lump sum now, since there is little realistic upside coming from new drilling. For a Smackover interest, especially one with a lithium component, the calculus is more nuanced because that production line could still be developing.

Either way we start from your actual statements, not a county-wide average, and walk you through how the offer reflects your well's specific decline and any new production terms before you decide anything. If you are unsure which category your check falls into, send it over and we will tell you plainly rather than guessing on the phone.

faqs.q: Is Fayetteville shale gas production coming back?
faqs.a: There is no significant new drilling activity in the field currently. Most operators moved capital to other basins years ago, so owners should plan around continued decline rather than a renewed drilling program.

faqs.q: What is the lithium line item on your Smackover royalty statement?
faqs.a: A small number of brine operators in the Smackover trend are now extracting lithium as a marketable byproduct, and some leases include royalty terms covering it. If this recently appeared on your statement, it reflects new production activity worth reviewing closely.

faqs.q: Your Smackover well is old. Is it still worth anything?
faqs.a: Older stripper wells often produce small but steady volumes for a long time, and that predictability is itself valuable in an offer, even though the gross production numbers look modest compared to a newer shale well.

faqs.q: Do you need to know which county your interest is in before contacting you?
faqs.a: It helps but is not required. Send us your most recent statement and we can identify the field and county from the operator and well information printed on it.

faqs.q: Should you sell now or wait to see how the lithium production develops?
faqs.a: That depends on how much of your total interest is tied to the lithium royalty versus the underlying oil and gas. If lithium production is still early on your specific tract, we discuss that uncertainty openly rather than pricing it as if it were already established.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Kansas
items.meta: Mississippian lime oil interest or Hugoton field gas royalty in Kansas? Decline pace differs a lot between the two. We build offers off your real statements.

sections.html:
Kansas has two very different stories running at once, a horizontal oil play that boomed and cooled fast, and a giant legacy gas field that has been declining slowly for generations.

The Mississippian lime play across south-central Kansas, Barber, Comanche, Harper, and Kingman counties among others, was drilled aggressively in horizontal wells starting around 2010, ran hot for a few years, and then slowed considerably as results came in more inconsistent than operators hoped. If your check traces to a lime well, you are likely watching a fairly steep decline from a well that peaked several years ago.

Down in the southwest corner of the state, Stevens, Grant, Seward, and Finney counties sit over the Hugoton field, one of the largest natural gas fields ever discovered in North America, first developed in the 1920s and still producing today at a fraction of its historic peak. That is a completely different rhythm, decades of gradual, well-understood decline rather than a boom-and-bust curve.

sections.title: The Mississippian Lime's Boom Already Happened
sections.html:
If your interest is tied to a horizontal Miss lime well, the peak production almost certainly already happened, usually within the first year or two after the well was drilled. What remains is the back half of that decline curve, still producing but at a fraction of the early rate, with limited new drilling in the play today.

That earlier boom-and-decline shape is important context for an offer. We look at how far along your specific well is in its decline rather than treating a Miss lime interest the same as a brand-new well just coming online.

sections.title: Hugoton Is a Slower, Longer Story
sections.html:
Wells in the Hugoton field have been producing for the better part of a century in some cases, and the decline curve there is famously gentle by comparison to almost any newer play. That longevity is part of why so many Kansas owners in the southwest corner of the state still see a check every month from a well drilled by their grandparents' generation.

Deductions on Hugoton gas checks reflect the gathering and processing network built up over decades to move that gas to market, so a lower net figure relative to gross volume is typical and not a sign of anything unusual.

sections.title: What to Check Before Deciding Anything
sections.html:
Pull your last six to twelve months of statements if you can. For a Miss lime interest, that window shows us how far into the decline curve the well already is. For a Hugoton interest, it confirms the slow, steady baseline that field is known for, which is exactly the kind of data that makes for a confident, well-supported offer.

If you are not sure which play your interest sits in, the operator name and legal description on your statement will usually tell us, and we can walk you through what that means for your specific situation.

sections.title: Selling Either Type of Kansas Interest
sections.html:
For a Miss lime interest well into its decline, selling often means capturing value now rather than watching a shrinking check continue shrinking. For a Hugoton interest, the calculus is different, a genuinely slow decline means the income stream could keep paying out steadily for years, so the decision comes down to what a lump sum is worth to you today.

Either way, we confirm ownership against the relevant county's records, prepare a mineral deed specific to your interest, and typically close within a few weeks of receiving signed paperwork. If you hold interests spread across more than one Kansas county, we can usually handle all of them together rather than running separate transactions.

faqs.q: Is the Mississippian lime play still being actively drilled?
faqs.a: Activity has slowed considerably since its early-2010s peak. Most current production comes from wells drilled years ago that are now well into their decline, with limited new drilling behind them.

faqs.q: Why has your Hugoton field check stayed roughly the same for years?
faqs.a: The Hugoton is known for an unusually gradual decline curve after nearly a century of production, so many owners see relatively stable, if modest, checks year over year rather than a sharp drop-off.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Kansas interest is Miss lime or Hugoton?
faqs.a: The county and operator name on your statement usually tell the story. South-central counties like Barber and Comanche point to Miss lime; southwest counties like Stevens and Grant point to Hugoton.

faqs.q: Does a steep decline on your lime well mean it's worth less?
faqs.a: Not necessarily worth less, just valued differently. An offer accounts for exactly where a well sits in its decline curve, so a lime well further into decline is priced against its remaining expected production, not its early peak.

faqs.q: Can you sell just your Hugoton interest and keep your Mississippian lime interest?
faqs.a: Yes. If you hold interests in both plays, each one is evaluated and sold independently, so you can choose to sell one, both, or neither depending on what makes sense for your situation.

faqs.q: Why do Kansas royalty checks sometimes list multiple wells on one statement?
faqs.a: Older Kansas units, especially in Hugoton, were often developed with multiple wells sharing a single spacing unit. Your statement may combine or separately list several wells that all draw from the same allocated interest.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Utah
items.meta: Utah Uinta Basin mineral owners in Duchesne or Uintah County: waxy crude pricing and takeaway capacity move your check more than most owners realize.

sections.html:
Uinta Basin oil is unusual crude, and if you don't know that going in, your check can look confusing for reasons that have nothing to do with the well itself.

Utah's oil and gas production centers almost entirely on the Uinta Basin, spanning Duchesne and Uintah counties in the northeastern part of the state. The crude produced there is famously waxy, thick enough that it can solidify at room temperature, which historically meant it had to move by heated tanker truck or specialized rail rather than standard pipeline. That transportation reality has a real, direct effect on what operators net for the oil, and by extension on your royalty check.

The royalty desk does not price a Uinta Basin interest without asking about takeaway, because a well producing the exact same volume can net very differently depending on how its oil gets to market.

sections.title: Uinta Basin Waxy Crude Economics
sections.html:
Because Uinta crude can't move through a typical cold pipeline without gelling, it's historically commanded a different, sometimes discounted, price relative to more standard grades, and required more expensive transportation to reach refining markets. Improvements in rail capacity and specialized handling over the years have helped, but the basin's crude still trades on its own dynamics rather than tracking a generic benchmark price one-to-one.

That's part of why we look at your actual net price per barrel on the statement rather than assuming it tracks whatever headline oil price is in the news that week.

sections.title: Duchesne and Uintah County Owners
sections.html:
Development in the basin has spread across both counties over the decades, with a mix of older conventional wells and newer horizontal activity in different pockets. Ownership here often traces back through agricultural and ranching families who held both surface and mineral rights on land homesteaded generations ago, which usually means more straightforward title work than states with heavily fractionated urban-adjacent ownership.

We still verify the specific legal description and chain of title carefully, since even rural family land can carry surprises after multiple generations of transfers.

sections.title: Split Estate With the Ute Indian Tribe
sections.html:
A meaningful portion of the Uinta Basin overlaps with the Uintah and Ouray Reservation, and mineral ownership there can involve tribal trust land, allotted interests, or federal administration alongside private fee minerals. If your tract touches any of this, the sale process involves additional review that a standard private mineral transaction doesn't.

We identify this early, since it changes both the timeline and the documentation needed to close cleanly.

sections.title: Rail Capacity and Why It Matters to Your Check
sections.html:
Because so much Uinta crude has historically depended on rail rather than pipeline, changes in available rail capacity, whether expansions or bottlenecks, can move the effective price operators receive and, downstream of that, your royalty. This is a basin-specific dynamic that doesn't show up the same way in a pipeline-connected play, and it's worth understanding before you compare your check to what you hear about other states.

We factor current takeaway conditions into how we think about a fair offer rather than pricing off assumptions from a different kind of basin.

faqs.q: Why does Uinta Basin crude sometimes sell for less than the price you see reported nationally?
faqs.a: Uinta crude is waxy and historically required specialized transportation rather than standard pipeline, which has affected its pricing relative to more common grades. We look at your actual net price on the statement rather than assuming it tracks a generic benchmark.

faqs.q: Does your mineral interest touch Ute tribal trust land?
faqs.a: It's worth checking, since a meaningful part of the Uinta Basin overlaps the Uintah and Ouray Reservation. If your tract involves tribal trust or allotted interests, the sale process includes additional review beyond a standard private transaction.

faqs.q: Is Uinta Basin production mostly old wells or new development?
faqs.a: Both. Duchesne and Uintah counties have a mix of older conventional wells and newer horizontal activity in different areas, so we look at your specific well's age and history rather than assuming either pattern applies.

faqs.q: Does rail capacity really affect what your royalty check pays?
faqs.a: Yes, since so much Uinta oil depends on rail rather than pipeline, changes in available capacity can move the effective price operators receive, which flows through to your royalty.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Utah mineral tract borders reservation land?
