faqs.a: The legal description on your deed or division order, cross-checked against Duchesne or Uintah county and Bureau of Indian Affairs records, usually settles it. We handle that check as part of reviewing any Uinta Basin interest.

faqs.q: Is Uinta Basin oil mostly conventional wells or horizontal development?
faqs.a: Both exist across the basin. Older conventional wells are common in longer-developed areas, while newer horizontal wells have been drilled in other pockets, so we look at your specific well type and vintage rather than assuming one or the other.

faqs.q: What documents speed up a Utah mineral rights sale?
faqs.a: A recent check stub or division order and any lease or deed you have on hand help most. If your tract touches tribal trust land, having whatever federal paperwork exists also shortens the review, though we can track it down if you don't have it.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Alabama
items.meta: Get an Alabama mineral rights offer from a buyer who reads Black Warrior coalbed methane statements for a living. Free review, no obligation to sell.

sections.html:
If your check comes out of Tuscaloosa, Fayette, or Walker County, it is almost certainly a coalbed methane gas check, and that changes how you should think about selling.

The Black Warrior basin is one of the oldest coalbed methane fields in the country, and it does not behave like a shale play. Wells were drilled mostly through the 1990s and early 2000s to dewater the coal seams and release trapped gas, and most of that drilling is long finished. What is left is a mature, slow-decline gas field with thousands of small royalty owners scattered across west-central Alabama, many of them heirs to interests their grandparents signed decades ago.

Oil & Gas Royalty Buyer brings years of operating-side experience with CBM production curves, and Alabama's are gentler than a shale well's cliff but they still trend one direction. That matters when you are deciding whether the check you get every month is worth more to you now, as a lump sum, than it will be worth stretched out over the next ten or fifteen years of gradual decline.

sections.title: Why an Alabama CBM Check Reads the Way It Does
sections.html:
Open a Black Warrior royalty statement and you will usually see one product code, not two. These are gas wells, produced water is a constant operating cost, and dewatering pumps are billed back against the well long after the coal seam has given up its early gas rush. That is a normal line item on these statements, not a sign something is wrong.

Deductions on Alabama gas checks tend to run heavier than on an oil check because gathering, compression, and dehydration all get subtracted before your royalty is calculated. If your net number looks small against the gross production volume printed above it, that gap is usually gathering and compression, not an error.

sections.title: The Decline Curve You're Actually Sitting On
sections.html:
Most Black Warrior CBM wells hit their peak gas rate years ago and have been declining at a slow, steady rate since. That is the nature of coal seam gas: no sudden cliff like a shale well, but also very little chance of a workover or infill well bringing a surprise increase. Operators in this basin are not drilling many new wells against these older units.

That combination, mature production with almost no new drilling upside, is exactly the situation where selling the income stream can make more sense than holding it. You are not giving up on a play about to take off. You are converting a shrinking, steady trickle into a number you control today.

sections.title: Heirship and Small Tracts Are the Norm Here
sections.html:
A large share of Alabama mineral owners we talk to inherited a fractional interest from a parent or grandparent who signed a lease decades before coalbed methane was even a common term. Interests get divided among siblings and cousins over a generation or two, and by the time it reaches you, the tract might represent a small percentage of a unit spread across several heirs.

That is not a disqualifier for selling. It just means the offer reflects your specific decimal interest, and we will walk through the division order with you so you understand exactly what percentage you own before any number gets discussed.

sections.title: What Actually Happens if You Decide to Sell
sections.html:
We start with your last few royalty statements, not a guess. Production history, the operator's reported decline, and current gas pricing all factor into how an offer gets built, and the range depends heavily on how the specific well or unit has been performing recently rather than any flat statewide number.

From there it is a straightforward transfer: a mineral deed, a title check against the county courthouse records in the county where your interest sits, and a closing timeline that usually runs a few weeks. You keep any payments that were already earned before closing; we take on the well's future decline from that point forward.

faqs.q: Why does your Alabama gas check vary so much month to month?
faqs.a: Gas price swings hit CBM checks harder than the underlying production volume does, since these wells produce a fairly steady gas rate. A cold winter spike or a summer price dip can move your check noticeably even when the well itself barely changed.

faqs.q: Is Black Warrior basin production still being drilled?
faqs.a: New drilling in the basin has slowed to a trickle compared to the 1990s and early 2000s buildout. Most current activity is workovers and dewatering pump maintenance on existing wells rather than new units, which is part of why the decline curve is so predictable.

faqs.q: Is a small fractional interest worth selling?
faqs.a: Small fractional interests are common in Alabama because of generational heirship, and they can still be sold. The offer is simply scaled to your decimal interest as shown on the division order, so a small percentage means a smaller number, not a declined offer.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to sell your mineral rights in Alabama?
faqs.a: You are not required to have one, but for larger or contested interests it is worth having an attorney review the mineral deed before you sign, particularly if the interest passed through an estate that was never formally probated.

faqs.q: How is your offer different from what your neighbor got?
faqs.a: Offers are built off the specific well or unit's recent production and decline, plus your exact decimal interest, so two neighbors on different wells within the same field can reasonably get different numbers even in the same county.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Mississippi
items.meta: Tuscaloosa Marine Shale acreage or Smackover, Norphlet legacy oil in Mississippi? We give you the honest read on each and a fair cash offer either way.

sections.html:
A decade ago, southwest Mississippi looked like it might become the next big shale story. It didn't quite happen, and understanding why matters for anyone holding acreage there today.

Around 2013 and 2014, operators moved into the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale across Amite, Wilkinson, and Adams counties with real ambition, drilling horizontal wells and hoping to replicate the success of plays like the Eagle Ford. The rock turned out to be more difficult and expensive to produce than hoped, and most companies scaled back or exited within a few years. If you signed a TMS lease during that window, you likely remember the excitement, and you may also remember how quietly it faded.

Further east, Mississippi's older story runs through the Smackover and Norphlet formations in counties like Jasper and Clarke, deep, often high-pressure oil and gas production that has been running for decades with far less fanfare but considerably more staying power than the TMS ever achieved.

sections.title: Being Honest About the TMS
sections.html:
If you are holding Tuscaloosa Marine Shale acreage in Mississippi hoping for renewed large-scale drilling, the realistic picture is that most operators who tried the play have moved on, and there is no broad indication that is changing soon. That is not the answer every owner wants to hear, but it is the one that leads to a fair offer instead of one built on speculation.

If your acreage does have production history, even limited, we look at that actual record. If it is undeveloped or leased but never drilled, that changes the conversation to what the lease itself, rather than a producing well, might be worth.

sections.title: Smackover and Norphlet: The Quieter, Steadier Story
sections.html:
These are deep formations, often produced through wells that were drilled decades ago and have settled into long, slow decline. Some of this production dates back to the mid-20th century, and interests have frequently passed through several generations of the same family since.

Because these are older leases in many cases, deduction language can vary more than you would see on a modern lease, so it is worth confirming exactly what your lease says about post-production costs before assuming your net check is calculated the same way a newer one would be.

sections.title: What Your Statement Actually Tells You
sections.html:
The county and operator name on your check are the fastest way to know which situation you are in. Amite, Wilkinson, and Adams point toward the TMS; Jasper, Clarke, and similar east-central counties generally point toward Smackover or Norphlet legacy production.

If you are holding a lease with no production at all, that is worth mentioning when you reach out too, since an undeveloped leased interest is priced very differently than one with an actual payment history behind it.

sections.title: Selling a Mississippi Interest, Developed or Not
sections.html:
For a producing Smackover or Norphlet interest, we build the offer from documented decline the same way we would anywhere else. For TMS acreage, whether producing, leased, or held-open, the conversation starts with an honest look at what is actually there rather than what the play was once expected to become.

Closing follows the standard path, a mineral or royalty deed and a title check through the chancery clerk's office in the county where the interest sits, typically wrapped up within a few weeks.

faqs.q: Is the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale being drilled in Mississippi right now?
faqs.a: Activity has been minimal for years after most operators scaled back or exited the play in the mid-2010s due to difficult geology and high costs. There is no broad current drilling program in the play.

faqs.q: Can TMS minerals be sold when leased but not producing?
faqs.a: Yes, though an undeveloped leased interest is valued differently than a producing one. We would look at your lease terms and any nearby activity rather than a production history that does not exist yet.

faqs.q: Why is your Smackover check so much steadier than what you hear about shale wells?
faqs.a: Smackover and Norphlet production in Mississippi is largely decades-old, mature production that settled into a slow, predictable decline long ago, unlike a newer shale well still working through its steepest early decline.

faqs.q: How do you find out which county your Mississippi interest is in?
faqs.a: Your royalty statement or lease should list the county and legal description. If you are unsure, send us what you have and we can help identify it from the operator and well information.

faqs.q: Will your TMS lease automatically renew if the operator never drilled?
faqs.a: That depends entirely on the lease's specific terms, primary term length, delay rental or shut-in provisions, and whether any of those conditions were met. Reviewing the actual lease language is the only reliable way to know its current status.

faqs.q: Are Smackover and Norphlet the same formation?
faqs.a: No, though they are often produced together in the same wells in parts of Mississippi. The Smackover is a limestone formation and the Norphlet a sandstone, sitting at different depths, and a single well can sometimes draw royalty from both.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Kentucky
items.meta: Small, fractional Kentucky mineral interest in eastern Appalachian gas or western Illinois basin oil? We sort out heirship and buy interests either side.

sections.html:
More than the geology, what usually complicates a Kentucky sale is the ownership itself, small tracts split among heirs, sometimes across three or four generations, on both ends of the state.

Kentucky's oil and gas country sits at the edges of two much bigger plays rather than in the middle of either one. Eastern Kentucky, around Pike, Floyd, and Knott counties, sits on the western fringe of the Appalachian basin, mostly small, older gas wells rather than the modern Marcellus-style horizontal drilling you see further north and east. Western Kentucky, around Union, Webster, and Henderson counties, sits on the eastern edge of the Illinois basin, legacy oil production with a long, quiet history.

In both regions, tracts tend to be small and family-held for generations, which means a lot of the work in selling a Kentucky interest is simply establishing who owns what before any number gets discussed.

sections.title: Eastern Kentucky Gas: Old Wells, Modest Volumes
sections.html:
Appalachian basin gas production in eastern Kentucky mostly predates the shale drilling boom that transformed Pennsylvania and West Virginia. These are typically shallower, older wells producing modest gas volumes on a slow decline, not modern horizontal Marcellus or Utica wells. If your check is small and has been small for a long time, that is consistent with this region's production profile.

Deductions here can vary depending on how old the underlying lease is, since some eastern Kentucky leases predate standardized post-production cost language by decades. It is worth confirming what your specific lease says before assuming your net number is calculated the same way a modern lease would be.

sections.title: Western Kentucky Oil: Illinois Basin's Southern Edge
sections.html:
Union, Webster, and Henderson counties sit on the same Illinois basin trend that runs up through southern Illinois, and production there follows the same pattern, older wells, often waterflood-assisted, producing small but steady oil volumes. It is unglamorous, dependable production rather than anything tied to a recent drilling boom.

If your check comes from this part of the state, expect a long, gradual decline with limited new drilling upside, which is the same honest read we would give an Illinois basin owner just across the state line.

sections.title: Heirship Is the Real Complication
sections.html:
Kentucky mineral tracts are frequently small to begin with and have often been divided among children and grandchildren without a formal probate ever clearing up who legally holds what percentage. It is common for us to find an interest split six or eight ways among cousins who have never discussed it with each other.

That is manageable, but it usually means gathering documentation, wills, prior deeds, sometimes an affidavit of heirship, before a sale can close cleanly. We walk owners through exactly what is needed rather than assuming everyone already has clear title in hand.

sections.title: What Selling Looks Like Once Ownership Is Clear
sections.html:
Once we can confirm your specific decimal interest, whether through a division order, a recorded deed, or probate documentation, we build an offer off recent production history for that well or unit, then prepare a mineral deed for the county where the tract sits.

Closing timelines run a bit longer than average when heirship documentation needs to be gathered first, but the process itself is the same straightforward deed-and-title-check sequence used anywhere else.

faqs.q: Your family's Kentucky interest was never formally divided among heirs. Can it still be sold?
faqs.a: Yes, though it typically requires gathering documentation like wills or prior deeds, or in some cases an affidavit of heirship, to establish clear ownership percentages before closing. We help identify exactly what is needed.

faqs.q: Is eastern Kentucky part of the Marcellus shale play?
faqs.a: Not really. Eastern Kentucky sits on the far southwestern edge of the broader Appalachian basin, but the modern Marcellus and Utica horizontal drilling boom concentrated mainly in Pennsylvania, West Virginia, and Ohio, not Kentucky.

faqs.q: Why is your western Kentucky oil check so small and steady?
faqs.a: Western Kentucky sits on the Illinois basin's southern edge, where production is largely older waterflood wells producing modest, stable volumes rather than anything from a recent drilling boom.

faqs.q: How many heirs can be involved in one Kentucky mineral sale?
faqs.a: We have worked through interests split among a dozen or more heirs. Each owner sells their own fractional share individually, so the number of co-owners does not prevent any one person from selling their piece.

faqs.q: What if your Kentucky lease was signed decades ago on a handshake with no formal recording?
faqs.a: That is more common than people expect in older Kentucky counties. We help track down whatever documentation does exist, county records, old check stubs, correspondence, to establish what can reasonably be confirmed before moving forward.

faqs.q: Is eastern Kentucky gas or western Kentucky oil worth more per interest?
faqs.a: Neither region is inherently worth more than the other in general terms. Value comes down to your specific well's production history and decimal interest, and modest, steady interests exist on both sides of the state.

faqs.q: Do you buy very small Kentucky interests, under one percent?
faqs.a: Yes. Given how common fractional heirship is across Kentucky's oil and gas counties, small decimal interests are the norm rather than the exception, and we price them the same way we would any other interest, scaled to what you actually own.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Tennessee
items.meta: Tennessee mineral owners on the Appalachian basin edge with small, older gas well interests: we'll give you a straight read on what a thin interest is worth.

sections.html:
Tennessee interests are almost always small, and the royalty desk states that up front rather than wasting your time with a call that ends in disappointment.

Tennessee sits on the far southwestern edge of the Appalachian basin, and its oil and gas history reflects that position, shallow, mostly conventional wells scattered across the Cumberland Plateau and parts of the eastern counties, developed over many decades rather than in a single modern boom. There's no Marcellus-scale horizontal play here. What exists is older, smaller, and quieter.

That doesn't mean a Tennessee interest has no value, but it does mean the conversation starts from a different baseline than a Texas or Oklahoma call, and the royalty desk sets that expectation early rather than allowing you assume otherwise.

sections.title: Tennessee's Small Legacy Wells
sections.html:
Most producing Tennessee wells are shallow conventional gas wells, many drilled decades ago and still on the books at low, steady volumes. Scott, Fentress, Overton, and Pickett counties on the Cumberland Plateau have the state's most concentrated legacy production, though even there individual wells are modest by the standards of a major shale play.

A check from one of these wells reflects that scale. It's usually a smaller monthly number than owners in bigger plays are used to hearing about, and that's simply the nature of Tennessee production, not a sign anything is wrong.

sections.title: What a Thin Interest Is Actually Worth
sections.html:
Small, older wells with long, flat production tails can still be priced fairly, but the math is different from a high-volume horizontal well. We look at your actual monthly production trend over as long a stretch as we can get, since a well that's been steady for fifteen years tells a more reliable story than a newer well still finding its baseline.

For owners with very small fractional interests, sometimes inherited many generations back, we're upfront that the offer will reflect that size honestly rather than inflating expectations.

sections.title: Cumberland Plateau Ownership Records
sections.html:
Tennessee mineral ownership on the Plateau often traces back through family land held for generations, with mineral rights sometimes severed decades ago and rarely revisited since. Title research here can mean working through older county register of deeds books rather than a modern digital system, particularly in the smaller rural counties.

We do that work as part of any offer, and it's routine for us even when it takes a bit more time than a state with newer, more centralized records.

sections.title: Why Buyers Are Selective in Tennessee
sections.html:
Because Tennessee lacks the density of active drilling seen in bigger plays, not every buyer in this market actively looks here, which can make it harder for an owner to get a second opinion on an offer. We do buy Tennessee interests, but we're honest that our pricing reflects the state's production profile, steady, modest, and mostly conventional, rather than treating it like a shale play it isn't.

If your interest genuinely has minimal production and thin history, we'll say so rather than stringing out a process that won't land anywhere useful.

faqs.q: Why is your Tennessee royalty check so much smaller than what you hear about in Texas or Oklahoma?
faqs.a: Tennessee production comes mostly from shallow, older conventional wells rather than large modern horizontal plays. Smaller, steadier checks are typical here and don't indicate a problem with your well.

faqs.q: Is your Cumberland Plateau mineral interest worth selling?
faqs.a: It depends on the well's production history and your fractional share. We review your actual production trend and give you a straight answer, including telling you if a sale doesn't make sense for a very thin interest.

faqs.q: Can old family-held Tennessee minerals still be researched?
faqs.a: Yes, we routinely work through older county register of deeds records in rural Tennessee counties. It can take a bit more time than a state with newer digital records, but it's a normal part of the process.

faqs.q: Do you actually buy Tennessee mineral interests, or just the bigger plays?
faqs.a: We buy Tennessee interests, though we're upfront that pricing reflects the state's steady, modest conventional production profile rather than shale-play assumptions that don't apply here.

faqs.q: What's the smallest Tennessee interest worth considering a sale on?
faqs.a: There's no hard cutoff, but very small fractional interests with minimal production sometimes aren't worth the paperwork for either side. We'll tell you plainly if that's the case for your specific tract rather than stringing along a process that won't land anywhere.

faqs.q: Are there any active shale plays developing in Tennessee now?
faqs.a: Not at meaningful scale. Tennessee's production remains dominated by older conventional wells on the Cumberland Plateau, and there's been no significant modern horizontal development comparable to nearby Appalachian states.

faqs.q: How do you determine a fair price for a small, steady Tennessee well?
faqs.a: We look at as long a production history as we can pull, since a well that's been flat and steady for a decade or more gives us a more reliable baseline than a shorter, noisier history. That baseline, along with your fractional share, drives the number.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Nebraska
items.meta: Own Nebraska minerals with no royalty check coming in, or a small one from the Niobrara/DJ basin edge? We evaluate non-producing and producing interests both.

sections.html:
Most of the Nebraska mineral inquiries the royalty desk receives aren't about a check at all, they're about a piece of paper that's never paid anything and an owner trying to figure out if it's worth keeping.

Nebraska sits on the far northeast edge of the DJ Basin and Niobrara play, and that geography matters more here than in most other states the royalty desk reviews. A handful of counties in the southwest corner, Dundy, Chase, Perkins, have seen real drilling tied to the same Niobrara chalk that's productive across the Colorado line. Most of the rest of the state's mineral ownership has never had a well drilled on it and probably never will.

That doesn't make the interest worthless, it just means the conversation is different from a Texas or Oklahoma call. The royalty desk explains plainly which situation you're in before discussing numbers.

sections.title: Nebraska's Place on the DJ Basin Map
sections.html:
The active edge of Nebraska's oil play sits in Dundy, Chase, and Perkins counties, tied into the same Niobrara and Codell formations that operators have worked hard across the border in Colorado's Wattenberg field. Wells here have been drilled in fits and starts depending on commodity prices and operator focus, so production history is choppier than in a core basin state.

If you're in one of these counties and have an active lease or a check coming, we look at the well's actual production, alongside its location relative to Colorado activity, before putting a number together.

sections.title: Non-Producing Doesn't Mean Worthless
sections.html:
Plenty of Nebraska mineral owners hold interests, often inherited from grandparents who homesteaded the land, that have never been leased or have sat under an old lease with no drilling. Those interests still have value, tied mostly to the possibility of future leasing activity and any bonus money that comes with it.

That value is lower and more speculative than a producing interest, and any honest buyer needs to say so upfront. We'll tell you if what you're holding is realistically a hold-and-wait situation or something worth cashing out of now.

sections.title: What a Nebraska Title Search Usually Turns Up
sections.html:
Because so little of the state has seen drilling, a lot of Nebraska mineral records haven't been touched since the original severance or a single estate transfer decades ago. That can mean thin paper trails, which is normal and workable, but it also means we sometimes find gaps that need a courthouse trip in the county seat to sort out.

We handle that research as part of any offer process. You don't need a clean, modern title file for us to get started, you need to know roughly where the property sits and what you believe you own.

sections.title: Setting Realistic Expectations on a Nebraska Sale
sections.html:
For producing interests in the southwest counties, we price against actual well performance the same way we would anywhere else. For non-producing acreage in the rest of the state, pricing is smaller and reflects speculative leasing potential rather than cash flow, and we say that directly rather than dressing it up.

Some owners decide a modest, certain payment today beats holding paper that may never pay a dime. Others decide to keep waiting. Both are reasonable, and we're not going to push you toward a sale that doesn't make sense for your situation.

faqs.q: Are Nebraska mineral rights worth evaluating if they have never produced a check?
faqs.a: Possibly, though value depends heavily on location relative to active drilling and any leasing history. We evaluate non-producing acreage differently than producing interests and will tell you honestly where yours likely falls.

faqs.q: Which Nebraska counties have actual oil production?
faqs.a: The active area sits mostly in Dundy, Chase, and Perkins counties in the state's southwest corner, tied to the DJ Basin Niobrara play that extends from Colorado. Most other Nebraska counties have little to no history of drilling.

faqs.q: Your family inherited mineral rights and nobody knows the legal description. What now?
faqs.a: Send us whatever documents exist, an old deed, a probate filing, anything with a legal description or county name, and we can usually trace ownership through county records from there.

faqs.q: Should you lease instead of selling your Nebraska minerals?
faqs.a: If your acreage is in an area seeing active leasing interest, that's worth exploring. If it's outside the productive trend, a lease offer may never come, and selling outright can be the more realistic path to getting value from the property.

faqs.q: How do you value Nebraska mineral rights that have never had a well drilled on them?
faqs.a: We look at proximity to active Dundy, Chase, and Perkins county drilling, any historical leasing bonuses paid in the surrounding township, and how the play has trended over recent years. It's a smaller, more speculative number than a producing interest, and we explain the reasoning behind it rather than just naming a figure.

faqs.q: Do you need a survey or professional appraisal before selling your Nebraska mineral rights?
faqs.a: No. We handle the title and production research ourselves as part of preparing an offer, so you don't need to pay for a separate appraisal or survey before talking to us.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Michigan
items.meta: Antrim shale gas check from the 1990s boom, or Niagaran reef legacy oil? Michigan interests are mostly mature. We buy them and explain the offer clearly.

sections.html:
If you've been holding a Michigan royalty interest since the 1990s, there is a decent chance you signed that lease during the original Antrim shale gas rush, long before shale drilling was a household term anywhere else.

Michigan's Antrim shale, concentrated in the northern lower peninsula around Otsego and Grand Traverse counties, was one of the earliest large-scale shale gas developments in the country, drilled hard through the 1990s using vertical wells and coalbed-style dewatering, well before horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing became the industry standard elsewhere. That makes Michigan's shale history genuinely older than most owners realize.

There is also a separate, even older legacy in the Michigan basin's Niagaran reef trend, small isolated oil and gas reservoirs scattered across the northern lower peninsula that have been quietly producing since the 1970s and 80s. Between the two, most Michigan mineral owners are sitting on production that peaked decades ago and has been sliding gradually ever since.

sections.title: The Antrim Boom Is Thirty Years in the Rearview
sections.html:
Antrim wells were drilled in a concentrated wave and, like most dewatering plays, took a few years to ramp to peak gas production before beginning a long decline. Most of those wells are now decades past their peak, producing a fraction of their original rate on a well-worn, predictable curve.

New Antrim drilling essentially stopped years ago as the play matured and operators moved on. If your check has been shrinking slowly for a long time without any sudden change, that tracks with exactly what this field has been doing for a generation.

sections.title: Reading an Antrim Statement
sections.html:
Antrim wells produce both gas and, notably, a fair amount of water, since dewatering the shale is what releases the gas in the first place. Water handling costs are a normal, recurring line item here, and they do not indicate a well is failing, just that it is doing what Antrim wells have always done.

Because these are older wells on older leases, it is also worth checking whether your specific lease predates common modern post-production cost language, since that can meaningfully change how deductions are calculated relative to a lease signed today.

sections.title: Niagaran Reef Interests Are a Quieter Story
sections.html:
Niagaran reef fields are smaller and more isolated than Antrim, individual reservoirs rather than one continuous formation, so production and decline can vary quite a bit from field to field even within the same county. Some of these fields have been producing steadily since the 1970s and 80s with very little fanfare.

If your interest is tied to one of these older reef fields, we look at the specific well's history rather than treating it like a typical Antrim interest, since the two production profiles do not necessarily move together.

sections.title: Selling a Legacy Michigan Interest
sections.html:
For most Michigan owners, the question is straightforward: the well is well past its peak, new drilling is not a realistic factor, and the choice comes down to a small but stable check continuing on the same gradual decline versus a lump sum today.

We build the offer from your actual recent statements, confirm ownership against the county register of deeds, most commonly in the northern lower peninsula counties where these fields sit, and typically close within a few weeks.

faqs.q: Why does your Antrim shale statement show a water disposal charge?
faqs.a: Antrim wells produce alongside significant water volumes because dewatering the shale is what releases the trapped gas. That cost is a standard, ongoing part of how these wells operate, not a sign of a problem.

faqs.q: Is anyone still drilling new Antrim wells in Michigan?
faqs.a: New drilling in the Antrim slowed to essentially nothing years ago as the play matured. Current production comes almost entirely from wells drilled during the original 1990s development wave.

faqs.q: What is a Niagaran reef and how is it different from Antrim?
faqs.a: Niagaran reef fields are isolated, individual oil and gas reservoirs scattered across Michigan's northern lower peninsula, distinct from the continuous Antrim shale formation. Production history can vary significantly from one reef field to the next.

faqs.q: Your check has been the same small amount for years. Is that normal?
faqs.a: For a mature Antrim or Niagaran interest, yes. These are old, slow-decline fields, and a small, fairly stable check is consistent with a well many years past its original peak.

faqs.q: What should an owner do after inheriting a Michigan interest without receiving statements?
faqs.a: Reach out to the operator listed on any old paperwork you have to confirm whether the well is still producing and whether your ownership was ever updated after the interest passed to you. We can help identify the operator from an old lease or division order if you are not sure.

faqs.q: Are Antrim leases from the 1990s different from modern leases?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many Antrim-era leases predate the standardized post-production cost and deduction language common in leases written today, so it is worth confirming what your specific lease actually says before assuming how deductions should be calculated.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Illinois
items.meta: Small, steady Illinois basin oil check from Wabash, White, or Marion County? We read waterflood statements every week and buy legacy interests outright.

sections.html:
Illinois basin checks are usually small, usually steady, and usually come from a waterflood unit that has been quietly producing for longer than most people realize.

Southeastern Illinois, Wabash, White, Lawrence, and the fields around Salem in Marion County, has been producing oil since before the First World War, and a huge share of what is still on production today runs through waterflood, injecting water into depleted reservoirs to push remaining oil toward the producing wells. It is unglamorous, low-volume work, and that is exactly why it has lasted this long.

If you hold an Illinois basin interest, you are likely looking at a small monthly check that has been remarkably consistent for years, sometimes decades. That consistency is the whole story here, and it is also what makes these interests genuinely valuable to price correctly rather than dismiss because the gross numbers look modest.

sections.title: Small Checks Are Not the Same as Worthless Checks
sections.html:
A $40 or $60 monthly check from a waterflood unit can look unimpressive next to what people hear about shale wells in Texas, but a steady $40 check that has held roughly flat for fifteen years is a very different asset than a $400 check on a well six months into a shale decline curve. Predictability has real value, and it is often underpriced by owners who assume small means unimportant.

We look at your full payment history when we can get it, rather than only the most recent statement, because a long, flat trend line is exactly the kind of data that lets us make a confident offer on a small legacy interest. That history is genuinely more useful to us than any single month's number, so it is worth digging out old statements if you have kept them.

sections.title: Reading a Waterflood Statement
sections.html:
Waterflood operating costs show up differently than a standard producing well because water handling and injection are ongoing expenses baked into the field's economics. If your statement shows a line for water disposal or injection costs, that is normal for this kind of secondary recovery and does not mean the well is struggling.

What matters more is the trend over several months. A waterflood unit that has held a stable volume for years is generally close to its natural sustained rate, and that stable rate is the anchor point we use when calculating an offer.

sections.title: Ownership Here Is Often Multi-Generational
sections.html:
Illinois basin production has been running long enough that a lot of current owners are third or fourth generation, and interests have been split among heirs repeatedly since the original lease. It is common for an owner to hold a fraction of a fraction, sometimes well under one percent of a unit.

That does not stop a sale from happening. We just need the division order or a recent statement showing your specific decimal interest so the offer reflects exactly what you own, not what the whole unit produces.

sections.title: Selling a Legacy Illinois Basin Interest
sections.html:
Because these fields decline so gradually, the case for selling usually comes down to what you would rather have: a small, steady check continuing indefinitely at roughly the same level, or a lump sum now that you can use for something with a clearer near-term purpose.

The process itself is simple. We confirm your interest against county records, most often in Wabash, White, Marion, or Clark County, prepare a mineral deed, and close typically within a few weeks once the paperwork is in order. Multi-generational ownership sometimes means a short delay while heirship documentation is gathered, but it rarely stops a sale from closing.

faqs.q: Your Illinois check is only $30 to $50 a month. Is it worth selling?
faqs.a: Yes, in many cases. What matters is the stability of that number over time, not the size. A long, flat production history on a small check is exactly the kind of asset we can put a fair number on.

faqs.q: Why does your statement mention water injection costs?
faqs.a: Most Illinois basin oil today is produced through waterflood, a secondary recovery method that injects water to push oil toward producing wells. The associated costs are a normal, ongoing part of that process, not a sign of a problem.

faqs.q: Can an owner sell a tiny fractional share of a unit?
faqs.a: Yes. Illinois basin ownership is frequently split many ways after generations of inheritance, and offers are simply scaled to your exact decimal interest as shown on your division order or statement.

faqs.q: Are new wells being drilled in the Illinois basin?
faqs.a: New drilling is limited today compared to the field's early-1900s buildout. Most current activity is maintaining and managing existing waterflood units rather than adding new wells.

faqs.q: What documents do you need to sell an inherited Illinois interest?
faqs.a: A recent division order or statement showing your decimal interest is the main thing, along with anything establishing how the interest passed to you, a will, a prior deed, or probate paperwork if it went through an estate.

faqs.q: Could your Illinois basin well be revived with new drilling technology?
faqs.a: It is possible in theory, but there is no widespread pattern of operators returning to old Illinois basin waterflood units with modern horizontal techniques. We price based on the well's actual current production rather than a hypothetical future workover.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Missouri
items.meta: Little to no current production on your Missouri mineral interest? We'll tell you straight what it's worth and buy it if there's a real number to offer.

sections.html:
The royalty desk states this plainly up front: most Missouri mineral interests we look at have little or no current production, and the honest thing to do is tell you that before we talk about a number.

Missouri sits on the eastern edge of the Forest City basin, a shallow, marginal formation that stretches up into Nebraska, Iowa, and Kansas. Far northwest Missouri, Nodaway and Atchison counties in particular, saw a wave of interest around 2008 through 2010 when coalbed methane operators tried to develop shallow coal seams there, similar to what had worked in other basins. It largely did not pan out at commercial scale, and most of that activity wound down within a few years.

There is also scattered, very old shallow oil production in pockets of the state, some of it dating back many decades, but Missouri has never been a major oil and gas producing state the way its neighbors are. If you inherited a mineral interest here, there is a real chance it has never produced a check, or stopped producing one a long time ago.

sections.title: Why So Little Missouri Acreage Is Actually Producing
sections.html:
The Forest City basin's coal seams and shallow reservoirs in Missouri simply did not deliver the volumes operators were hoping for during the coalbed methane push. Compared to more productive basins, the economics here were marginal even during the height of interest, and most companies that leased acreage in the late 2000s let those leases lapse rather than drill them out.

That means a lot of Missouri mineral owners are holding an interest with no active well attached to it at all, just a historical lease that expired or a family record of minerals that were reserved generations ago and never developed.

sections.title: If You Do Have an Active Check
sections.html:
For the smaller number of owners who do get a statement, usually from an older shallow oil well or a legacy coalbed methane unit still limping along, the volumes tend to be modest and the decline has generally already flattened out at a low, stable level rather than actively falling further.

In that situation, we treat it the same as we would any other legacy interest, we look at the actual production history and build a number around what the well has genuinely been doing, not around what Forest City basin acreage was once hoped to become.

sections.title: If You Don't Have an Active Check
sections.html:
If your mineral interest has never produced, or hasn't in a long time, there usually is not much of a cash offer to make on the mineral rights themselves, and we will tell you that directly rather than stringing out a conversation. What can still have value in that situation is simply getting the interest off your estate paperwork, particularly if you are trying to clear title on a piece of land for sale or settle an estate cleanly.

We are candid about this because owners in Missouri, more than almost any other state we cover, reach out expecting a check that the underlying geology just does not support right now.

sections.title: Figuring Out Which Situation You're In
sections.html:
The fastest way to know is simple: have you received a royalty check in the last year or two, and do you have any statement or division order showing an operator's name? If yes, send it over and we will review the actual production. If no, tell us what you know about how the interest came to you, an old family deed, a mineral reservation from a land sale, and we can tell you honestly what your options look like.

Either way, you will get a straight answer, not a runaround, because a marginal Missouri interest deserves the same honest read as a productive one anywhere else.

faqs.q: Why has your Missouri mineral interest never produced anything?
faqs.a: Much of northwest Missouri saw coalbed methane leasing interest around 2008 to 2010 that ultimately did not develop into commercial production. Many leases from that era expired without a well ever being drilled.

faqs.q: Is Missouri a real oil and gas producing state?
faqs.a: Not at meaningful scale compared to its neighbors. There is scattered legacy shallow oil production and some limited Forest City basin activity, but Missouri has never been a major producer, and most acreage sees no active drilling.

faqs.q: Can you sell mineral rights that have never produced a check?
faqs.a: There is typically little market value in undeveloped Missouri minerals on their own. We will tell you plainly if that is your situation rather than offering a number the underlying production does not support.

faqs.q: What if you just want the interest off your estate paperwork?
faqs.a: That is a legitimate reason to sell even a non-producing interest, particularly during estate settlement or a land sale where clean title matters. Ask us about that specifically and we can discuss options.

faqs.q: Are there any active operators currently drilling in Missouri?
faqs.a: Activity is limited and concentrated mostly in the far northwest corner of the state. We can check whether any operator is currently active on your specific tract once we have your legal description or a recent lease.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in California
items.meta: San Joaquin or Los Angeles basin legacy oil interest? California mineral rights are old, regulated, and slow-declining. Get an offer built off your history.

sections.html:
A California mineral interest usually traces back a long way, often a lease first signed before your grandparents were born, and that history is exactly what shapes what it is worth today.

California oil production is some of the oldest in the country. Kern County and the greater San Joaquin Valley around Bakersfield have been producing continuously since the early 1900s, and the old Los Angeles basin fields, Signal Hill, Long Beach, Wilmington, built entire neighborhoods around drilling activity that is still quietly running today, often from wells you would never notice from the street.

What that means for an owner is a state where almost nothing is a new shale play chasing a boom. It is legacy stripper production, waterflood and steam-flood secondary recovery keeping old fields alive, and a regulatory environment that has made new permitting slow and increasingly rare. Your check is a piece of that long, patient history, and it should be valued that way.

sections.title: A State Where New Drilling Has Nearly Stopped
sections.html:
California has made new oil and gas permitting difficult for years now, and that trend has only tightened. Practically speaking, that means the wells producing your interest today are very likely the same wells that will still be producing it, in decline, for the foreseeable future. There is essentially no scenario where a new pad shows up next door and your check jumps.

That is not necessarily bad news for a seller. It makes the decline curve unusually predictable, which is exactly the kind of production history that lets us build a confident offer rather than guessing at future activity that simply is not coming.

sections.title: Steam Floods and Secondary Recovery on Your Statement
sections.html:
Much of the San Joaquin's heavy oil, particularly around Kern River and Midway-Sunset, is only economic because of steam injection, cyclic steaming or steamflood, that thins the oil enough to flow. That process costs money, and you will often see it reflected in higher operating cost deductions than a conventional light-oil well would carry.

If your net check looks thin relative to the gross barrels reported, steam and lifting costs on a heavy oil field are usually the reason, not a mistake on the statement.

sections.title: Los Angeles Basin Interests Carry Their Own History
sections.html:
If your interest sits in the old LA basin fields, Signal Hill, Wilmington, or similar legacy urban oil fields, the lease itself is often decades old with terms that read very differently from a modern shale lease. Some of these leases predate standardized post-production cost language entirely.

Pulling the original lease, or at least confirming with the operator what version of the lease governs your interest, is worth doing before selling, since it directly affects how deductions get calculated on your check.

sections.title: What Selling a Legacy California Interest Looks Like
sections.html:
We start with several months of your actual statements to see the real decline rate on your specific well or unit, since California fields vary enormously in how gently or quickly they decline. From there, an offer is calculated from that documented history, not a flat per-acre number that ignores how old and specific these leases are, and we walk you through exactly how the two connect before any figure is put in front of you.

Closing involves a mineral or royalty deed and a title check through the county recorder where the interest sits, most commonly Kern or Los Angeles County. The timeline usually runs a few weeks, and you keep anything already earned on production before the closing date. Older leases occasionally take a little longer to confirm because early recording practices in some of these fields were less standardized than they are today.

faqs.q: Are new wells being drilled in California right now?
faqs.a: New permitting has slowed dramatically statewide, so most current production comes from existing wells rather than fresh drilling. Owners should generally plan around a long, gradual decline on already-producing wells rather than expecting new activity.

faqs.q: Why are your deductions higher than a friend's Texas royalty check?
faqs.a: Heavy oil fields in California often require steam injection to produce, and that added cost typically shows up as higher operating deductions than you would see on a conventional light-oil well elsewhere.

faqs.q: Your lease is decades old. Does that matter for selling?
faqs.a: It can. Older California leases sometimes use different cost-bearing language than modern leases, which affects your net royalty calculation. We review the specific lease terms before finalizing an offer.

faqs.q: Is your Los Angeles basin interest worth less because it's an urban field?
faqs.a: Not inherently. Urban legacy fields like Signal Hill and Wilmington have produced steadily for decades and are valued on production history and decline, the same as any other California field.

faqs.q: Could California permitting rules affect an existing well's future decline?
faqs.a: Regulatory pressure in California generally slows new drilling more than it changes the natural decline of an already-producing well. We factor documented decline into an offer, but permitting risk is worth understanding as separate context for the state overall.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Alaska
items.meta: Alaska royalty ownership is unusual, ANCSA corporations, state land leases, North Slope allocation. Get a straight read on your interest and a cash offer.

sections.html:
North Slope royalty ownership rarely looks like the small private-mineral-owner situation you'll read about in Texas or Oklahoma, and any buyer you talk to should say that upfront.

Alaska is the odd state in this business. Very little North Slope production sits under privately owned minerals the way it does in the Lower 48. Most of the acreage is state land leased under Alaska's own royalty framework, and a meaningful share of what is privately held runs through Alaska Native corporations formed under the 1971 land settlement, not individual family mineral deeds.

That said, private and inherited interests do exist, particularly overriding royalty interests, net profits interests tied to older Cook Inlet production, and small non-operating positions some owners picked up decades ago. If you are holding one of those and getting a check, the questions worth asking are different than in a typical Lower 48 shale state.

sections.title: Figure Out What Kind of Interest You Actually Hold
sections.html:
Before anything else, we need to know whether your paperwork describes a fee mineral interest, an overriding royalty carved out of someone else's lease, or a net profits interest. Alaska has all three floating around from decades of Cook Inlet and legacy North Slope deals, and each one is valued differently because each one sits in a different spot in the payment waterfall.

If your statement comes from a Cook Inlet operator rather than a North Slope one, that is worth noting too. Cook Inlet is older, smaller, and declining at a different pace than the giant North Slope fields, and offers reflect that basin difference.

sections.title: Why North Slope Checks Can Look Unusually Stable
sections.html:
The major North Slope fields have been producing for decades with disciplined reservoir management, so decline rates on legacy production tend to be gentler than a typical shale well's. That stability is part of what makes a long-held override or net profits position worth pricing carefully rather than guessing at.

It also means the decision to sell is less about racing a cliff and more about weighing a steady but shrinking payment against a lump sum you can use, invest, or pass on now instead of over another decade or two of gradual decline.

sections.title: ANCSA and Corporate Land Complicate a Straight Sale
sections.html:
If your interest traces back to an Alaska Native corporation or a settlement trust rather than a personal mineral deed, transferring it is not a standard courthouse recording the way it is in most states. There are additional restrictions and, in some cases, shareholder or trust approvals involved, and we tell owners this directly rather than promising a quick deed transfer that Alaska law does not actually allow for that category of interest.

For interests that are freely transferable, private overrides and net profits interests, the process looks much closer to a normal sale: verify the interest, review recent statements, and put together a mineral deed or assignment specific to that interest type.

sections.title: What We Need From You to Get Started
sections.html:
Send the most recent division order or check stub you have, along with anything identifying the field, whether it says Prudhoe Bay, Kuparuk, or a Cook Inlet unit name. That single piece of information tells us more about how to value your interest than almost anything else you could provide.

From there we tell you plainly whether your interest is the kind we can move on quickly or whether it involves a corporate or trust layer that needs its own review before any number gets discussed. We would rather spend an extra week confirming what category your interest falls into than rush you into paperwork that a title company later flags as unworkable.

faqs.q: Can you sell mineral rights you inherited through an Alaska Native corporation?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific corporate or trust structure involved. Some ANCSA-related interests carry transfer restrictions that a standard mineral deed cannot get around, so we review the underlying documents before telling you what is actually possible.

faqs.q: Why is your Alaska royalty check labeled as an override, not a straight royalty?
faqs.a: Many Alaska private interests were created as overriding royalty interests carved out of an operator's working interest in older Cook Inlet deals, rather than as a fee mineral interest tied to the land itself. The label on your statement usually tells you which kind you hold.

faqs.q: Is North Slope production declining like Lower 48 shale wells?
faqs.a: Not at the same pace. Major North Slope fields have been managed for decades of sustained output, so the decline curve is generally slower and steadier than what you would see on a typical shale well within its first few years.

faqs.q: Do you need to be an Alaska resident to sell?
faqs.a: No. Ownership and residency are separate questions. Plenty of owners we work with inherited an Alaska interest while living somewhere else entirely, and that has no bearing on whether the interest can be sold.

faqs.q: Why did you get a Permanent Fund Dividend but no separate mineral check?
faqs.a: The Permanent Fund Dividend is a state distribution funded broadly by Alaska's oil revenue and has nothing to do with owning a private mineral or royalty interest. If you hold an actual interest, it should generate its own separate statement from an operator, not a state agency.

items.name: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
items.meta: A letter shows up offering to buy your minerals out of nowhere. Before you sign or ignore it, here's how to read the offer and check if it's actually fair.

sections.html:
An envelope shows up offering to buy minerals you'd nearly forgotten you owned, and the honest question isn't whether to trust it, it's whether the number inside is even in the right neighborhood.

Mailbox offers on mineral interests are a real business, not automatically a scam, but the number on the page is written by someone who wants to buy low, same as any other buyer would. That's not sinister, it's just the incentive built into the letter. The problem is most owners have no way to check that number against anything, since they don't have another royalty check to compare it to and don't know what similar interests nearby have sold for.

The royalty desk has reviewed plenty of these letters for owners over the years, and the pattern is consistent: some are close to fair market value, some are well below it, and almost none of them explain how the number was calculated. That last part is what you should be asking about before you do anything else.

sections.title: Why buyers mail these offers in the first place
sections.html:
Companies that send unsolicited mineral offers are usually working from county deed records, cross-referenced against operator production data, targeting owners in areas with active drilling. They're playing a numbers game, sending out volume with the expectation that some percentage of recipients will accept without shopping the offer around. That's a legitimate business model, but it means the first number offered is rarely the best number available.

It also means the letter often arrives with real urgency language, deadlines, 'this offer expires,' pressure to respond quickly, designed to keep you from comparing it against anything else before deciding.

sections.title: Reading the offer for what it actually pays
sections.html:
Look for what the offer is actually based on: does it reference your specific well or lease, your decimal interest, and recent production, or is it a generic form letter with blanks filled in? An offer grounded in your actual production history is worth taking seriously. A generic offer with no specifics is a starting point at best, not a real valuation.

Also check whether the offer covers all of your interest or just a portion, since some letters are deliberately vague about exactly what's being purchased until you call in, at which point the terms can shift.

sections.title: Getting a real number to compare it against
sections.html:
The only way to know if an unsolicited offer is fair is to get at least one independent quote based on your actual check history or division order. That quote should reference the same production data the original offer claims to be based on, which lets you compare apples to apples instead of guessing. If a second buyer's number lands meaningfully higher on the same underlying production, you've learned something real about the first offer.

There's no obligation to respond to an unsolicited letter on any particular timeline, regardless of what the deadline language says. Taking a week or two to get a second opinion costs you nothing and tells you exactly what you're dealing with.

sections.title: What to do if the offer turns out to be fair
sections.html:
Not every unsolicited offer is a lowball. Some buyers mail competitive numbers precisely because they know owners are increasingly likely to shop the offer around, and a fair first offer saves everyone time. If a second quote comes back close to the original number, that's a reasonably strong sign the first offer was already priced fairly.

Either way, read the actual purchase and sale agreement carefully before signing, checking exactly what interest, well, and county it covers, since the specifics in the contract matter more than anything printed in the original letter.

faqs.q: Is it safe to respond to an unsolicited offer for your mineral rights?
faqs.a: Generally yes, responding to ask questions doesn't obligate you to sell. Just verify the company's identity independently before sharing sensitive information, and don't sign anything until you understand exactly what interest and terms are being offered.

faqs.q: Why would a buyer offer less than your minerals are actually worth?
faqs.a: Volume-mailed offers are priced to be profitable for the buyer across many owners, and the initial number is rarely their best offer. Getting a second quote based on your specific production history is the way to find out if you're leaving money on the table.

faqs.q: Do you have to respond by the deadline printed on the letter?
faqs.a: No, deadline language in these letters is a sales tactic, not a legal requirement. You're free to take the time you need to get a second opinion before responding either way.

faqs.q: What should you ask the company that sent the offer?
faqs.a: Ask exactly what interest they're offering to buy, what production data or well the number is based on, and whether the offer covers all or part of your interest. Vague answers to specific questions are worth noting.

faqs.q: Can you negotiate an unsolicited offer instead of just accepting or rejecting it?
faqs.a: Yes, the first number in the letter is a starting point, not a final price, and most buyers expect some negotiation, especially once you've shown you've gotten a comparison quote elsewhere.

faqs.q: Should you be worried if you get several unsolicited offers for the same interest?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, receiving multiple letters usually just means several buyers are working the same county's deed records. It's actually useful, since you can compare the numbers directly instead of trying to benchmark a single offer against nothing.

items.name: Inherited Mineral Rights
items.meta: A royalty check shows up with your late relative's name on it, or a check register with no explanation at all. Here's how to make sense of what you inherited.

sections.html:
Most people who inherit mineral rights find out the hard way, either a check arrives made out to a parent who passed, or nothing arrives and they have to go find out what's even out there.

One early inherited-royalty file involved an owner whose father had passed two years earlier. The checks kept getting mailed to his address, which had a new owner living in it who'd been quietly cashing nothing but tossing the envelopes, unaware they even mattered. She lost two years of payments simply because nobody updated the operator's records. That's the most common failure point with inherited minerals: not the value of the asset, but the paperwork gap between generations.

If you've inherited an interest, producing or not, the first job is getting yourself on record as the legal owner. Everything else, whether to keep it, lease it, or sell it, comes after that.

sections.title: Getting the interest into your name
sections.html:
Operators pay whoever the county records show as the current owner, so if the deed or lease is still in a deceased relative's name, the checks either stop or go into suspense until someone proves ownership. Depending on your state, that proof is usually either a probated will, an affidavit of heirship, or a small estate affidavit for modest estates. This is where a probate attorney earns their fee, even on a small interest, because getting it wrong means resubmitting paperwork to every operator involved.

Once title is cleared, you'll file a new division order with each operator paying on the property. That's the document that sets your net revenue interest and gets checks flowing to you directly.

sections.title: Figuring out what you actually own
sections.html:
Start with whatever paper trail exists: old check stubs, a 1099, a lease document, or a deed referenced in the estate file. If there's nothing, the county clerk's office in the county where the land sits can pull the deed history, and most operators will tell you your decimal interest over the phone once you've established you're the legal owner. Don't assume a lack of recent checks means the interest is worthless; leases lapse and get renewed, and wells go through periods of low activity between workovers.

It's also worth checking whether the mineral rights were severed from any surface land your relative owned, since heirs sometimes inherit the surface and assume the minerals came with it when they didn't, or vice versa.

sections.title: Keep, lease, or sell
sections.html:
If the interest is producing steadily and you're comfortable with ongoing paperwork, K-1s or 1099s, and the uncertainty of decline, holding it can make sense, especially if there are multiple heirs who want to keep something in the family. If the interest is small, scattered among several siblings, or you'd rather have one number today than an unpredictable stream for years, selling converts it into something easier to divide and closes the estate cleanly.

There's no wrong answer here, but the math is worth doing honestly: add up what the checks have actually paid over the last two or three years, look at the trend, and weigh that against a lump sum offer before deciding either way. If multiple heirs inherited together, this conversation is worth having as a group early, since a sibling who wants to hold and a sibling who wants to sell can both get what they want if the interest is divided and sold in pieces rather than forced into one shared decision.

sections.title: What check history tells you before you decide
sections.html:
Before making a keep-or-sell decision, pull together whatever check stubs or 1099s exist and look at the pattern over time rather than any single month. A steady or slowly declining trend suggests a mature, well-understood well. Sharp swings often just reflect commodity price movement rather than anything wrong with the property itself.

If the well is relatively young, decline can still be steep in the early years before leveling off, which is normal and worth understanding before assuming a falling check means the asset is losing all its value.

faqs.q: How do you find out if you inherited mineral rights you didn't know about?
faqs.a: Check the deceased's county property records in the county where they owned land, and look through their old tax returns for 1099-MISC or 1099-NEC forms from oil and gas operators, which is often the first sign a royalty interest exists.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to transfer inherited mineral rights into your name?
faqs.a: In most states you'll need some form of probate document or affidavit of heirship to clear title, and an attorney familiar with mineral title in that state is worth the cost even on a modest interest, since a mistake can delay payments for months.

faqs.q: Can you sell mineral rights before the estate is fully settled?
faqs.a: Usually not until the executor or administrator has authority to transfer the asset, or until it's distributed to heirs individually, though the exact timing depends on your state's probate process.

faqs.q: What if several siblings inherited the interest together?
faqs.a: Each heir typically owns an undivided fractional share and can decide independently whether to keep or sell their portion, though many families find it simpler to make the decision together and close one combined transaction.

faqs.q: Is inherited mineral income taxed differently than other inherited assets?
faqs.a: Mineral interests generally get a stepped-up basis at inheritance, which affects any future sale, and ongoing royalty income is taxed as it's received. Talk to your CPA or attorney about how this applies to your specific estate before filing.

faqs.q: What if the checks stopped years before you even knew you would inherited anything?
faqs.a: Stopped checks usually mean the operator moved the payments into suspense once mail started bouncing, rather than the interest going dormant on its own. Once you're established as the legal owner with a current address, most operators will release suspended funds owed to you, sometimes going back several years, subject to their own escheatment timelines.

items.name: Fractional & Small Interests
items.meta: A 1/64th interest split among cousins isn't worth managing for most owners. Here's why fractional interests happen and what selling a small share looks like.

sections.html:
Somewhere in Oklahoma or West Texas there's a courthouse file showing forty people own a piece of a quarter section, and most of them have no idea their check is even smaller than it should be.

Fractional interests are what happen when land gets passed down for three or four generations without anyone consolidating it. A tract that started with one owner in the 1940s can end up divided among grandchildren and great-grandchildren, each holding a sliver so small the resulting royalty check barely covers a tank of gas. The royalty desk has reviewed division orders listing an owner's interest as something like 0.0009 net revenue interest, and the operator still has to cut and mail that check every month, or hold it in suspense if the address is wrong.

None of this makes the interest worthless. It makes it hard to manage, hard to sell for a fair number without the right buyer, and easy for owners to lose track of entirely.

sections.title: How interests end up this small
sections.html:
It's almost always inheritance math. A parent's interest splits evenly among children, then each child's share splits again among their kids, and by the third generation what started as a whole mineral estate is scattered across a dozen or more owners, some of whom may not even know they hold anything. Add a divorce, an out-of-state move, or a name change along the way, and the operator's division order department has a real puzzle keeping everyone paid correctly.

Some fractional interests also come from old term assignments or partial sales decades ago, where a prior owner sold half their minerals and kept half. Either way, the size of the interest doesn't tell you much about the quality of the underlying acreage. A tiny fraction of a good spacing unit can still be worth more than a large interest in acreage nobody's drilling.

sections.title: Why small interests are a headache to hold
sections.html:
The paperwork burden doesn't scale down with the interest size. You still get a 1099 every year, still have to keep your address current with every operator paying you, and still have to respond if a lease renewal or division order correction shows up in the mail. For an interest paying a few dollars a month, that's a lot of overhead for not much return.

Fractional interests are also the hardest for heirs to divide further. If four cousins jointly inherit an already-small interest, splitting it again among their own children eventually produces fractions so thin that no operator wants to keep cutting checks for them, and the interest can end up in unclaimed property or state suspense accounts instead.

sections.title: What a check on a fractional interest tells a buyer
sections.html:
Small doesn't mean unreadable. If you've got even six months of check stubs or a 1099, the royalty desk can usually explain what the underlying decimal interest is worth without needing an attorney to run title first. What matters is the net revenue interest, the well or wells it's tied to, and whether that production is holding steady or declining.

Buyers who specialize in fractional interests exist specifically because most large buyers won't bother with a sub-1% share. If you're being told an interest is too small to matter, that's usually a sign you're talking to the wrong buyer, not that the interest has no value.

faqs.q: Is it worth selling a mineral interest that only pays a few dollars a month?
faqs.a: It can be, depending on how many years of production remain and how the underlying well is performing. A small monthly check adds up over a decade, and a buyer will typically quote a lump sum tied to that trailing production rather than dismiss it as too minor.

faqs.q: How do you find out how small your interest actually is?
faqs.a: Your division order or most recent check stub will list your decimal interest, usually a number like 0.00125. If you don't have a recent statement, the operator's owner relations department can usually pull it up if you give them your name and the well or lease name.

faqs.q: Your interest is shared with several cousins. Can you sell just your share?
faqs.a: In most cases yes, since mineral interests are typically owned as undivided tenants in common, meaning each owner can sell their own share independently without needing the others to agree.

faqs.q: Will consolidating with your cousins get us a better price than selling separately?
faqs.a: Sometimes, since a buyer may offer a small premium for acquiring a larger combined block in one transaction, but it depends on the buyer and isn't document. It's worth asking, but don't let coordination delays cost you months if some heirs aren't responsive.

faqs.q: What if your fractional interest isn't currently producing?
faqs.a: Non-producing fractional interests are harder to value and typically sell for less, since there's no check history to price against. Some buyers still purchase them based on the county, the operator's activity nearby, and whether the acreage is currently under lease.

items.name: Minerals in Probate & Estates
items.meta: Mineral interests are one of the more confusing assets an executor has to deal with. Here's where they fit in an estate, and how to sell one to close probate.

sections.html:
Executors handle bank accounts and houses all the time, but a mineral interest with an unfamiliar decimal number on a division order is usually the first one they've ever seen.

If you're the executor or administrator of an estate that includes mineral rights, you're carrying two responsibilities at once: getting an accurate value for the estate's inventory and tax filings, and eventually distributing or liquidating the asset for the beneficiaries. Both of those are harder with minerals than with a bank account, because value isn't a static number on a statement, it moves with production trends and lease activity.

The good news is that estates deal with mineral interests often enough that the process is well established, even if it's new to you personally. It usually comes down to inventory, valuation, and a decision about whether to distribute the interest to heirs or sell it and distribute cash.

sections.title: Where minerals sit in the estate inventory
sections.html:
Mineral and royalty interests get listed in the estate inventory like any other asset, valued as of the date of death for both probate and any estate tax purposes. That date-of-death value matters later too, since it typically sets the beneficiaries' stepped-up basis for future capital gains if the interest is eventually sold.

Getting that valuation right sometimes means pulling a formal appraisal, especially for larger estates, but for smaller interests a documented market quote based on production history around the date of death is often sufficient. Talk to the estate's attorney or CPA about what your specific jurisdiction requires.

sections.title: An executor's options for the interest
sections.html:
Depending on the will's instructions and the beneficiaries' wishes, an executor generally has authority to either distribute the mineral interest in kind to the heirs, splitting the decimal interest among them, or sell the interest and distribute the cash proceeds instead. Selling is often preferred when there are multiple beneficiaries who don't all want to co-own a fractional interest going forward, or when the estate needs liquidity to cover debts, taxes, or final expenses.

If the will doesn't specifically address the mineral interest, most states allow an executor with general sale authority to sell estate assets, including minerals, as long as it's in the beneficiaries' interest and properly documented.

sections.title: Selling to close the estate
sections.html:
A mineral sale during probate works like any other, with the added step that the buyer will want to see the letters testamentary or letters of administration proving you have legal authority to sign on the estate's behalf. Have that document ready along with recent check stubs or a division order before you start getting quotes, since it shortens the process significantly.

Executors are often working against a deadline, whether that's a court date to close probate or pressure from beneficiaries wanting resolution, so a straightforward cash sale with a clean, fast closing tends to serve the estate better than a drawn-out negotiation. Getting more than one quote before signing anything also gives you something concrete to point to if a beneficiary later questions whether the executor got a fair price for the estate.

sections.title: Coordinating with beneficiaries along the way
sections.html:
Even where formal consent isn't legally required, keeping beneficiaries informed before a mineral sale closes tends to prevent disputes later. A short written update explaining the offer received, the production history it's based on, and the reasoning for selling rather than distributing in kind goes a long way toward avoiding a challenge after the fact.

If beneficiaries disagree about whether to sell, that disagreement is worth resolving before closing rather than after, since an executor who moves forward over a beneficiary's clear objection is taking on more risk of a later challenge to the sale.

faqs.q: Can an executor sell mineral rights without all beneficiaries agreeing?
faqs.a: In many cases yes, if the will grants general sale authority or the court has approved the sale, but requirements vary by state and by the specific will's language. Confirm your authority with the estate's attorney before proceeding.

faqs.q: How is a mineral interest valued for estate tax purposes?
faqs.a: Typically at fair market value as of the date of death, based on production history and market activity at that time, similar to how any other income-producing asset is valued for an estate.

faqs.q: What documents does a buyer need from an estate to close a sale?
faqs.a: Letters testamentary or letters of administration showing your authority to act for the estate, a copy of the deed or division order for the interest, and recent check stubs or a 1099 if the interest is producing.

faqs.q: Is it better to sell mineral rights during probate or distribute them to heirs first?
